Gate One is one binary in front of your applications. Everything else — an identity provider, the optional broker, the token broker, Redis — is a separate component you choose to run. See Components for a page per component.

All releases attach a single services_<version>_src.tar.gz containing the auth-bridge and token broker sources. They are not part of the gate-one binary: each runs as its own container.
Minimal install Gate One + one OIDC provider + a TLS reverse proxy.
Download a release (gate-one_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz from the release page or a signed dist/), verify it (see Publish and trust a plugin for the trust model), and extract it.
Write api-routes.json — start from Direct OIDC or Keycloak with Google.
Validate, then start:
export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... # the authProvider.clientSecretEnv variable gate-one -check -config api-routes.json gate-one -config api-routes.json # listens on :3000 Put it behind the reverse proxy — TLS, the public host, and the OIDC callback URL. See Reverse proxy.
Probe it — /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness).
Optional components cladone-auth (embedded IAM) — configure it and point Gate One at it with authProvider.type: "oidc".
auth-bridge — the reference implementation of the HTTP bridge contract, used with authProvider.type: "http-bridge".
Token broker — the service behind delegated credentials, declared in tokenBroker.
Redis — shared state required only for several replicas.
What is not a component A Backend-For-Frontend is your application behind a backend: route, not a Gate One service (see Plugins).
Keycloak, Postgres and other platform services are yours to run; Gate One only needs an OIDC issuer (and Redis for HA).
Runnable deployments The source repository ships two prepared deployments:
[deploy/local/](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local) — demos on *.localhost: no domain and no external account. Four run without Docker (embedded dev provider); four run the real OIDC chain with Docker Compose and a local demo identity provider. Every runnable [example](/docs/examples/) links its demo.
[deploy/vps/](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/vps) — the production shape: Traefik with Let’s Encrypt, Gate One, cladone-auth and Google, ready to copy to a VPS.
Both mount prebuilt binaries from $BIN_DIR; neither builds Gate One. Besides gate-one and cladone-auth, the demos use gate-one-demo-idp — a fake OIDC provider shipped with each release and never to be used in production.

Gate One is one binary. A complete deployment adds a few separate services around it: a reverse proxy in front, an identity provider, and — depending on the features you enable — the optional cladone-auth embedded IAM, a bridge, the token broker and Redis for shared state.
Component Role Required? Guide Gate One The gateway: route policy, session, proxy, MCP, injection yes Install Identity provider Identification and (optionally) authorization claims yes IAM and providers Reverse proxy TLS termination, routing, load balancing recommended Reverse proxy cladone-auth Optional embedded IAM / OIDC issuer (IdP federation, grants) optional cladone-auth auth-bridge Reference implementation of the http-bridge contract optional auth-bridge Token broker Per-user delegated credentials for upstream calls optional Token broker Redis Shared session/revocation state for several replicas only for HA Redis The components that return identity or IAM facts — cladone-auth and the HTTP bridge contract — are the ones people confuse. cladone-auth is an OIDC issuer reached with authProvider.type: "oidc"; the bridge is a request-verification service reached with http-bridge. See IAM, IdPs and provider types for the side-by-side.

SSO across your apps Useful if you want one login for several applications without changing the applications.
One authentication provider, one login host and a shared cookie domain across applications.
Feature Example SSO across different domains Useful if your applications live on unrelated domains and you want one IdP login without a second form.
ssoGroups declares the shared OIDC/client/session settings once, one provider per domain, and routes.hosts expands one route body across those domains.
Feature Example Multiple identity providers Useful if your users come from several identity providers and you already run an IAM.
Use Keycloak, Zitadel or another OIDC IAM to federate Google and other IdPs behind one issuer.
Feature Example Embedded IAM Useful if you want IdP federation and managed user grants without running an external IAM.
The lightweight cladone-auth embedded IAM maps IdP claims to a common roles/scopes/claims model and manages local and federated users.
Feature Example Horizontal scaling Useful if you need several Gate One replicas behind a load balancer.
Shared Redis session/revocation state and a common signing key make logout and revocation effective across replicas.
Feature Example Protect APIs and MCP tools Useful if you expose APIs or MCP tools to authenticated users and machine clients.
Route-level identity conditions, JWT/JWKS validation for APIs, and MCP protected-resource metadata with audience and scope checks.
Feature Example Expose REST APIs and MCP servers as MCP tools Useful if you want MCP clients to reach services that do not speak MCP.
Derive tools from an OpenAPI document, proxy an existing MCP server, and aggregate several services under one endpoint with its own audience, scope and identity.
Feature Example Call services with the user's credentials Useful if a route or an MCP tool must call an external service as the signed-in user.
The token broker stores a per-user token; upstream.delegated injects it into API and MCP requests, and the user badge links to the connections page.
Feature Example Injectable UX Useful if you cannot modify the frontend but need a user badge, a guard, gated controls or a PWA shell.
HTML/JS/CSS injection, declarative UI gating, a 403 banner and a strict CSP — without touching the application source.
Feature Example Bring your own account panel Useful if you own the application UI and want the account details in your own burger menu.
Read the Gate One session probe and render the user, roles, scopes and claims without the built-in badge.
Feature Example Usage events and plugins Useful if you need metering, audit, observability, or a commercial extension.
Durable per-type WAL, signed out-of-process plugins, targeted 503 on backpressure and an opaque subjectId instead of user data.
Feature Example Cloudflare Turnstile on any form Useful if you want to stop bots on a public form, including a page Gate One already proxies.
One platform-wide block injects the widget into forms or gates whole pages/actions with a signed 30-minute clearance cookie.

Gate One extensions are out-of-process services. The gateway talks to them over HTTP/JSON; it never loads a third-party authentication provider and never calls a plugin on the authentication path.
Plugin families Family Runs in Transport Decides auth? Licence Auth adapter
IAM
HTTP/JSON
yes, in the IAM
Gate One licence
Injection / userscript / UI
Gate One
route inject bundle (config)
no
extension licence
Event consumer
Gate One
HTTP/JSON, signed manifest
no
extension licence
The injection bundle and the event consumer are extensions; auth adapters stay in the IAM and remain under the Gate One licence.
A Backend-For-Frontend is not a plugin: it is a proxied backend: route, post-auth by definition (it receives the identity DTO / X-Gate-One-Subject), and can be written in any language. Gate One never loads it. Response transforms are the gateway’s native injector chain (inject, rewriteBody, responseHeaders, rewriteRedirects, the guard); bespoke logic belongs in the backend or the edge proxy, not in a plugin.
Invariants A plugin never decides whether a request is authenticated.
no pre-auth hook; the plugin is called after checkAuth/checkMCPAuth;
no self-registered route; it attaches to a compiled route;
immutable identity DTO, never the mutable *http.Request;
reserved headers (Authorization, Cookie, X-User-, X-Gate-One-, X-Forwarded-*) are stripped before any outbound call;
auth, securityHeaders, license, rateLimit and quota are out of scope;
internal network only, signed assertion on every call, separate UID, no secrets in the environment, egress allow-list.
Specific tests enforce that an anonymous request, an invalid token or a missing scope never reaches the plugin.
Event consumer contract The plugin exposes two endpoints:
Endpoint Purpose GET /health
readiness; a failing health check stops new batches
POST /events
batch [{offset, event}]; commit, then acknowledge
Every call carries:
X-Gate-One-Assertion: base64url(payload).base64url(HMAC-SHA256) The payload binds the audience (plugin name), an expiry and the body size. The plugin must verify it before processing the batch.
The event schema is published at usage-event.schema.json and documented in the reference. The user is an opaque subjectId; no token, cookie, email or username is present.
Manifest { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "extension", "name": "com.cladone.audit", "version": "1.0.0", "apiVersion": "v1", "hostAPI": ">=1.0 <2.0", "keyId": "example-2026", "artifact": { "type": "binary", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 84, "platform": "linux/amd64" }, "capabilities": ["events"], "events": { "types": ["auth", "error"], "filters": { "statusClasses": ["4xx", "5xx"] }, "maxLagBytes": 5000000, "onMaxLag": "block" }, "signature": { "alg": "ed25519", "keyId": "example-2026", "value": "base64url…" } } The signature covers the canonical JSON with signature zeroed, plus the artefact digest. For an extension the manifest also carries the event subscription and the optional licenseFeature.
See the manifest reference for every field.
Trust store The trust store is the local allow-list. It is provisioned out-of-band (signed lock file, package manager, embedded key) and never fetched from the plugin.
{ "keys": { "example-2026": "base64url-ed25519-public-key" }, "allowedNames": ["com.cladone.*"], "allowedDependencies": {}, "revokedDigests": [], "allowAuth": false, "coreVersion": "1.5.0" } The loader verifies the signature, artefact digest and size, dependencies, revocation, host API, kind and event subscription. For a local sidecar it verifies before starting; for a remote service it verifies the manifest and the image/attestation, and authenticates the channel.
See the trust-store reference.
The publisher can also publish a signed publisher feed listing compatible components and revocations; the operator adopts it with publisherFeed. See Publish and trust a plugin.
Configuration { "usage": { "dir": "./usage-wal", "nodeId": "gw-1", "subjectSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_SUBJECT_SECRET", "pluginSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET", "trustStore": "trust-store.json", "types": { "auth": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "always" }, "error": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "window_ms", "windowMs": 250 } }, "plugins": [{ "name": "com.cladone.audit", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9100", "manifest": "audit.manifest.json", "artifact": "audit-echo.placeholder" }] } } usage.trustStore is required when a plugin uses a signed manifest. Relative paths (manifest, artifact, trustStore, dir) are resolved from the configuration file. After editing, SIGHUP reloads the configuration and recreates the gateway, including its plugins; an invalid file is refused.
A plugin can also be installed as a descriptor file instead of an inline entry: set usage.pluginsDir (conventional name plugins.d) and every *.json file in it is one plugin entry, merged with usage.plugins (inline first). Relative manifest/artifact paths are resolved from the descriptor, so a plugin directory is self-contained. Duplicate names are refused, and usage.requireSigned applies to discovered plugins exactly as to inline ones. The directory is rescanned on SIGHUP.
Reference plugin cmd/plugin-audit-echo is the reference consumer. It verifies the assertion, decodes the batch and logs the events; it has no dependency on Gate One internals.
export GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET=... go run ./cmd/plugin-audit-echo -addr :9100 -name com.cladone.audit The complete signed example is routes.json, audit.manifest.json, trust-store.json.
The publisher/operator walkthrough — develop unsigned, sign, install and revoke — is in Publish and trust a plugin.
What is not a plugin an authentication provider inside Gate One (type: "plugin" is rejected);
a mutable request or identity hook before authentication;
a self-registered route;
a replacement for securityHeaders, license, rateLimit or quota;
a compile-time Go module distributed as a third-party plugin.
Licence The licence terms (core, plugin exception, PLUGIN-LICENSING.md) are summarised under Source and licence.

Gate One protects applications as a reverse proxy, but it should itself sit behind a front reverse proxy or ingress controller in most deployments (Traefik, nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer).
Why Gate One listens on plain HTTP and does not manage certificates. The ingress terminates TLS, renews certificates and applies HSTS.
One public entry point gives OIDC redirect URIs, cookie domains and MCP metadata a stable URL that is independent of the container address.
The ingress load-balances and health-checks the Gate One replicas, so the container port never has to be published.
WAF rules, rate limits, request-size limits and access logs stay in front of Gate One instead of competing with its own route policy.
Only the ingress needs to know where Gate One runs; clients cannot reach it directly.
Forwarded headers Gate One reads the incoming scheme, host and X-Forwarded-* headers when it rewrites backend redirects and computes rate-limit identities. The ingress must set:
X-Forwarded-Proto — the client scheme;
X-Forwarded-Host — the public host;
X-Forwarded-For — the client address chain.
Because those headers are trusted from the immediate hop, Gate One must not be reachable directly by clients. Publish only the ingress.
Minimal configurations Three complete examples, smallest first. Each terminates TLS, passes the public host, sets X-Forwarded-* and streams responses. The files live in examples/reverse-proxy/ (Caddy, Traefik and nginx), next to a validate.sh that parses them with the real implementations.

Useful if you want to… give users one login for several applications;
keep the applications untouched: no SDK, no OIDC library, no frontend patch;
share a session between app.example.com, reports.example.com and similar hosts;
revoke a session centrally and have every application refuse it on the next request.
Gate One is a reverse proxy: the application still receives a normal HTTP request. It never sees a token unless you ask for it.
What the user sees The first visit to any protected host redirects to the login host. After the identity provider callback, Gate One sets one session cookie on the shared parent domain. Every other Gate One route on that domain accepts the same session, so the user does not log in again.
According to the route, the application receives an identity:
X-Gate-One-Subject (opaque, stable per user and issuer) when usage events are enabled;
the identity headers configured by the auth provider;
the original Authorization header only when the route explicitly delegates it.
What actually enables SSO Three things together:
the same authentication provider verifies both routes;
a shared cookie domain (cookieDomain) covers every application host;
both routes are served by the same Gate One deployment.
Adding a second route alone does not create SSO. Replacing the provider alone does not create SSO either. The second application must use the same provider and share the same session cookie domain.
The complete sequence and configuration are in the multi-app SSO example.
Logout and revocation The RP session lifetime is Gate One’s own (sessionTtlSeconds, one hour by default), independent of the identity provider’s short ID-token lifetime. Logout clears the cookie and records the revocation:
RP-initiated logout uses the provider’s end_session_endpoint;
back-channel logout is validated and persisted;
a revoked sid/sub is refused on the next request.
A revocation covers only sessions and tokens issued before it: a new sign-in after a logout is accepted — a user is never locked out by their own logout — while a copied cookie from before the logout still fails.
The revocation TTL defaults to the issuer’s advertised refresh-token lifetime, or 30 days. It is never shorter than the session TTL.
Register the logout redirect at the IdP RP-initiated logout sends the originating application as post_logout_redirect_uri. Register every application host as a valid post-logout redirect URI:
Keycloak: client → Valid post logout redirect URIs, one https://app.example.com/* per application host;
the embedded IAM: tenants[.postLogoutRedirectUris] (empty falls back to redirectUris, the login host only).
If the IdP rejects that URI it shows an error and does not end its SSO session. Gate One’s own session is gone, but the next visit finds the IdP session and signs the user straight back in — so login looks "refused" even though no error is shown.
Troubleshooting Symptom Cause Invalid redirect uri at logout
the application host is not a registered post-logout redirect URI
signed back in immediately after logout, or login "refused" without an error
the IdP SSO session was not ended because its post-logout redirect was rejected
"Login session expired" right after returning from the IdP
the sign-in took longer than the transaction window (15 minutes), or a second sign-in in the same browser replaced it
Operational notes Same parent domain required. cookieDomain must cover every application host. app.company.com and app.other.com cannot share a cookie. For unrelated domains, use cross-domain SSO: each domain keeps its own cookie and the IdP session provides the single login.
Secrets never in the file. Use clientSecretEnv.
Several replicas? See Horizontal scaling for the shared-state requirement.
Important Gate One does not create users, passwords or refresh tokens; that is the identity provider’s job (or the optional embedded IAM).
A route can bind only one authentication provider. Multi-provider hosting uses authProviders + auth.provider and one provider per route. Cross-TLD SSO uses ssoGroups + routes[].hosts so the shared provider settings are declared once.
Applications that need the raw access token must opt in; by default tokens are never forwarded.

Do I need this guide? Gate One does not add a Content Security Policy unless a route declares a csp block. If you only proxy a page through Gate One, with no csp block and no custom injection, there is nothing to do: the page’s own policy (if any) passes through unchanged.
your situation what to do page proxied by Gate One, no csp block, no custom injection, and the page sends no CSP
nothing: Gate One adds no CSP.
page proxied, but the page already sends a CSP
the browser enforces it. The guard’s inline script/style must be allowed by that policy, or the guard is blocked. Configure Gate One csp.mode: "merge" (script hashes) or "nonce", and make the app’s style-src compatible with the guard style. See “An application that already has a CSP”.
you enable csp on a route
this guide applies.
you inject custom HTML/CSS/JS (inject, userscripts, plugins)
this guide applies: your injected content must satisfy the policy.
you proxy an external site that sends a CSP
both policies are enforced; the origin’s policy can block the guard. See “External sites and upstream”.
You need this guide in the last four cases.
What Gate One injects For a frontend route with the guard active, Gate One adds:
an inline <script> (the guard: session probe, login recovery, UI gating, user badge);
a <style> element created at runtime by the guard, carrying the CSP nonce of the response;
optionally PWA wiring (manifest link, service worker registration) and custom injections from the route bundle.
Since the guard’s UI is entirely class-based, it does not set style="…​" attributes and does not need 'unsafe-inline'. The one runtime <style> is nonced from document.currentScript.nonce.
The four modes mode behaviour off
Nothing is emitted or amended. The origin’s policy (if any) is the only one.
merge
The origin policy is preserved; the gateway only appends the hashes of its own injected scripts and of the guard stylesheet to script-src-elem / script-src / default-src and style-src-elem / style-src / default-src. No policy of its own. This is the default for a proxified external site that already sends a CSP.
hash
Gate One emits its own policy; the guard script and the guard stylesheet are allow-listed by SHA-256 hashes, and explicit script-src / style-src sources apply. The body is not rewritten.
nonce
Gate One emits its own policy with a per-response nonce and stamps inline <script> tags. The guard’s runtime <style> carries the same nonce. This is the recommended mode for applications that accept a per-response nonce.
own: true removes the origin’s Content-Security-Policy (and -Report-Only) headers and lets the gateway’s policy be the only one. It is opt-in, logged, and only valid with mode: "nonce" or "hash" and reportOnly: false. Use it only for a site you control/accept and for which the configured policy is complete. Without own, the origin policy remains enforced in addition to the gateway’s.
reportOnly: true emits Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: the policy is evaluated and violations are reported, but nothing is blocked. Use it to roll out a policy without breaking the site.
Nonce semantics — read this before enforcing In nonce mode, Gate One stamps every inline <script> in the HTML response (unless it already carries a nonce). This includes the application’s own inline scripts and any custom injection. As a consequence:
it removes the need for 'unsafe-inline' in script-src;
it does not protect against a <script> injected into the HTML by a server-side vulnerability, because that script is stamped too.
If you need protection against server-side HTML injection, use the hash or merge mode with a strict origin policy, and keep application scripts in external files.
stampScripts:
absent / inline (default): only <script> tags without src are stamped; external scripts stay governed by the host allow-list;
all: every <script> tag is stamped (only meaningful with a host allow-list or 'strict-dynamic').
Styles: the real constraint CSS has two different mechanisms, and only one accepts a nonce:
mechanism controlled by nonce? <style>…</style>
style-src-elem (falls back to style-src)
yes
style="…" attribute
style-src-attr (falls back to style-src)
no
A nonce (or hash) never applies to a style attribute. To obtain a strict policy without 'unsafe-inline':
use external CSS files (style-src 'self');
use classes instead of element.style / style="…​";
let Gate One nonce or hash its own runtime <style> (it already does: nonce in nonce mode, guard-stylesheet hash in hash/merge mode);
for third-party widgets that insist on style attributes, isolate the exception with style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline' rather than relaxing the whole style-src.
Gate One’s guard follows this rule: badge, banners, chips and gating states are classes; hidden gated elements use [data-gtw-gated-off]{display:none}. A static test fails the build if an inline style reappears in the guard.
Application checklist for styles no style="…​" attributes (including generated by JS);
no element.style = …​ / .style.cssText / .style.display;
use classList and classes, or an external stylesheet;
no <style> without a nonce (the gateway does not stamp application <style> tags; move them to a CSS file);
SVG style attributes are style attributes too;
third-party embeds: check whether they need style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'.
Scripts and event handlers A strict script-src without 'unsafe-inline' also blocks:
onclick="…​" and other inline event handlers (script-src-attr);
javascript: URLs;
eval(), new Function(), setTimeout("code") ('unsafe-eval');
document.write of scripts without a nonce/hash.
Use addEventListener, external scripts and data attributes.
With nonce mode, inline <script> tags are stamped by the gateway, so existing inline scripts work — but see the server-side injection caveat above. For the strictest setup, move scripts to external files and rely on script-src 'self' only.
A strict configuration Start report-only:
"csp": { "mode": "nonce", "reportOnly": true, "directives": { "default-src": "'none'", "script-src": "'self'", "style-src": "'self'", "img-src": ["'self'", "data:"], "font-src": "'self'", "connect-src": ["'self'", "https://auth.cladone.com"], "worker-src": "'self'", "frame-ancestors": "'none'", "object-src": "'none'", "base-uri": "'none'", "form-action": "'self'" } } Why these directives:
directive role default-src 'none'
deny by default; every resource type must be explicitly allowed.
script-src 'self'
external same-origin scripts; the gateway adds its nonce and hashes.
style-src 'self'
external same-origin styles; the gateway adds its nonce.
img-src
add data: only if the application uses data-URI icons.
font-src
self-hosted fonts; add the font CDN if used.
connect-src
fetch, XHR, EventSource and WebSocket endpoints. Add the IdP origin if the application calls it directly.
worker-src
the PWA service worker ('self').
frame-ancestors 'none'
anti-clickjacking.
object-src 'none', base-uri 'none'
remove plugin/base-tag injection vectors.
form-action 'self'
restrict form destinations.
Keep reportOnly: true until the reports are clean, then switch to false. A policy that emits violations is not protecting the page in report-only mode.
For a site that you control and whose origin CSP is structurally incompatible (e.g. hosts pinned to the origin), Gate One can own the policy:
"csp": { "mode": "nonce", "own": true, "directives": { "...": "a COMPLETE policy for this site" } } own removes the origin’s Content-Security-Policy and -Report-Only headers, logs a warning, and cannot be combined with reportOnly: true. Do not use it for a site you do not control.
Reading violations The gateway serves a collector (default /__gate-one_csp/report) and logs one line per violation:
CSP VIOLATION host="app.example.com" directive="style-src-elem" blocked="inline" document="https://app.example.com/" source="..." line=572 Typical signatures:

Browser DevTools also shows the violating element and the computed policy; the gateway log is the aggregate view across users.
An application that already has a CSP If the application (or the proxified origin) sends its own Content-Security-Policy, the browser enforces both policies: the application’s and Gate One’s, whichever is stricter.
For scripts, csp.mode: "merge" appends the SHA-256 hashes of the guard and other gateway-injected scripts to the origin’s script-src-elem / script-src / default-src. The origin policy does not need 'unsafe-inline' for the guard.
For styles, merge appends the SHA-256 hash of the guard’s stylesheet to the origin’s style-src-elem / style-src / default-src. The guard’s runtime <style> is then allowed by hash, without 'unsafe-inline', and the origin policy stays in place. The guard stylesheet is deterministic per route (static classes + the route’s uiGate selectors), so the hash is stable and cache-friendly.
This covers the guard, not the application’s own inline styles: style="…​" attributes and application <style> tags still need to be refactored to classes/external CSS (or covered by the application’s own nonce/hash). If the origin policy says style-src 'none', the gateway appends the guard hash, so the guard style is allowed while the origin’s other restrictions remain.
nonce mode still adds the gateway’s nonce for the guard style; the origin policy is not amended with that nonce (a per-response nonce cannot be known by the origin), but the guard stylesheet hash is appended by merge/hash/nonce modes via the origin amendment.
own: true is the explicit alternative when the origin policy is fundamentally incompatible: the origin headers are removed and only the gateway policy applies. Use it only for a site you control/accept and with a complete policy.
External sites and upstream For a proxified external site that already sends a CSP, the browser enforces both policies: the origin’s and the gateway’s, whichever is stricter. Gate One never removes or weakens the origin policy.
Consequences:
merge appends the hashes of the guard script and of the guard stylesheet to the origin’s script-src-elem and style-src-elem (fallbacks script-src/style-src/default-src). A strict origin policy no longer blocks the guard, without 'unsafe-inline'.
if the origin policy is incompatible for another reason (hosts pinned to the origin, script-src 'none' for the site’s own code, etc.), use own: true or upstream.responseHeaders.remove only for a site you control/accept, and provide a complete policy;
upstream.responseHeaders.remove is still a blunt tool: it is not logged by the CSP layer and removes the origin’s protections. Prefer merge or own.
external sites that use inline styles themselves will need style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline' or a refactor you do not control.
The guard is handled by hash; the remaining difficulty is the site’s own content, not the guard. Document the exception per route.
PWA, MCP, SSE and WebSocket PWA: worker-src 'self' for the service worker; manifest-src 'self' if your policy declares it; the Workbox runtime is self-hosted. A CSP nonce is per response: a cached HTML page keeps its nonce, so the cached response must keep the matching CSP header. Workbox caches the response headers with the body; verify this after a cache version change. For long-lived cached HTML, hash mode is more cache-friendly than a per-response nonce.
MCP: the MCP endpoint is same-origin (/mcp); connect-src 'self' is enough for HTTP. If an MCP client uses a WebSocket, add its origin.
SSE (EventSource) and WebSocket are governed by connect-src, not script-src.
IdP redirects: login is a top-level navigation, not connect-src; form-action applies only to forms, not to location.href.
Rollout procedure Enable reportOnly: true with the strict directives.
Load the main pages; watch the browser console and the gateway CSP VIOLATION logs.
Fix one directive family at a time (styles first: they are the most common).
Re-run the UI smoke tests and a real navigation with a session.
Switch reportOnly: false only after a clean period.
Keep a rollback: reportOnly: true (or mode: "off") can be applied by SIGHUP without a restart.
Minimal test commands # the header actually emitted (nonce changes per response) curl -sD - -o /dev/null https://app.example.com/ \ | grep -i '^content-security-policy' # aggregate violations docker logs <gate-one-container> 2>&1 | grep 'CSP VIOLATION' # route-level validation gate-one -config api-routes.json -check Known limitations Gate One does not stamp application <style> tags; use external CSS.
Style attributes cannot be nonced: classes or style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'.
In nonce mode, all inline scripts are stamped; it is not a defense against server-side HTML injection. Use hash/merge plus a strict origin policy.
A proxified external site’s CSP is enforced in addition to the gateway’s; an incompatible origin policy can block the guard.
Third-party widgets may require a documented style-src-attr or script-src exception.
Gate One’s own UI (guard, badge, banners) is strict by construction and does not require 'unsafe-inline'.

body:
cladone-auth is the optional embedded IAM: a small OIDC issuer and user directory that federates external IdPs, maps their claims to a common roles/scopes/claims model and stores per-user grants. It lets you offer IdP federation and managed users without running Keycloak, Zitadel or another full IAM.
Gate One reaches it as an ordinary OIDC issuer: authProvider.type: "oidc" with issuer pointing at the IAM.
What it is, and what it is not It is an OIDC issuer/IAM: IdP federation, a user directory, claim mapping, grants, Ed25519-signed tokens, JWKS, discovery and the revocation keyspace Gate One reads.
It is not a full IAM suite: no admin UI, no multi-identity linking, no per-resource policy engine.
It is not an http-bridge: it does not implement the HTTP bridge contract.
It is optional: for a single IdP, point Gate One straight at that issuer and skip the IAM.
Run it cladone-auth is a single Go binary, shipped signed with each release. It reads its own configuration file (tenants, upstreams, mappings, local accounts, session store):
cladone-auth -check -config embedded-iam.json cladone-auth -config embedded-iam.json Then point Gate One at it:
{ "authProvider": { "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://login.example.com", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET" } } Redis is optional for the IAM and required only when several IAM instances share session/revocation state.
Where to go next Embedded IAM — why and how, with the claim-mapping model.
Embedded IAM example — a runnable IAM + Gate One configuration.
Embedded IAM configuration reference — every embedded-iam.json field.

Useful if you want to… give users one login across app-a.com and app-b.fr;
keep one cookie per domain instead of trying to share a cookie across unrelated registrable domains;
declare the OIDC/client/session settings once and avoid divergent copies;
declare the application route body once when the backend is the same.
Gate One cannot set one cookie for app-a.com and app-b.fr: browsers reject a Domain that is not a suffix of the current host. Cross-TLD SSO therefore relies on the IdP session, exactly like the multi-subdomain case relies on cookieDomain.
What the user sees app-a.com -> login.app-a.com -> IdP (session already exists) -> callback -> Gate One session for app-a.com app-b.fr -> login.app-b.fr -> same IdP (same session) -> callback -> Gate One session for app-b.fr There is one redirect per domain, but no login form while the IdP session is valid. If the IdP session is expired, the normal interactive login is required. This is not a handoff protocol and it does not create a cross-TLD Gate One cookie.
Configuration The shared settings live once on the ssoGroups entry. Only the domain-specific fields are repeated in providers[]:
{ "ssoGroups": [{ "id": "company", "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "scopes": ["openid", "profile", "email"], "roleClaims": ["roles"], "sessionKeyEnv": "OIDC_SESSION_KEY", "sessionStore": { "type": "redis", "url": "redis://redis:6379/0", "passwordEnv": "REDIS_PASSWORD", "prefix": "cladone:auth:v1:" }, "backchannelLogout": true, "providers": [ { "id": "app-a", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.app-a.com", "cookieDomain": "app-a.com", "defaultAppUrl": "https://app-a.com/" }, { "id": "app-b", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.app-b.fr", "cookieDomain": "app-b.fr", "defaultAppUrl": "https://app-b.fr/" } ] }], "defaultAuthProvider": "app-a", "routes": [{ "hosts": ["app-a.com", "app-b.fr"], "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } providers[] only accepts id, loginBaseUrl, loginUrl, cookieDomain, cookieName, redirectUrl, defaultAppUrl, links and mcpAudience. A shared field such as issuer, clientId or sessionStore placed in a provider is rejected by the strict decoder.
routes[].hosts[] expands one route body into one concrete route per host; auth.provider is inferred from the provider whose cookieDomain covers the host. hosts is mutually exclusive with host and wildcard.
Why Redis is required for a multi-domain group Each domain has its own Gate One session cookie. A group with more than one provider must use sessionStore.type: "redis" with the same sessionKeyEnv on every provider: the revocation state (and the sub/sid global logout) is then shared, so a logout on app-a.com is refused on app-b.fr on the next request.
Without shared state, app-b.fr can keep accepting its local cookie until it expires even after a logout on app-a.com.
A provider’s defaultAppUrl is used when someone visits that provider’s login host root; it overrides the global defaultAppUrl and must point to a route of that provider (or a host under its cookieDomain).
IdP setup Register every callback:
https://login.app-a.com/auth/callback
https://login.app-b.fr/auth/callback
If you use back-channel logout:
if the IdP allows one URL per client, point it at one login host and keep the same issuer and Redis revocation prefix on every provider. The receiving Gate One instance revokes the session in the shared store; the other domain checks that store on the next request;
if the IdP supports one URL per client only and the stores are not shared, this single URL cannot cover both domains: use a second client or a group-level subject revocation instead.
Both domains must use the same issuer and the same user identity (issuer + sub). If you use different IdPs per domain, the IAM’s account linking is not enough yet: Gate One’s subjectId is per (issuer, sub).
Important Zero form, not zero redirect: the IdP round-trip remains.
The IdP must reuse its own session; Gate One sends the provider’s default prompt.
A cookie is never shared across TLDs; logout propagation relies on back-channel logout or the shared Redis revocation state.
With IAM local accounts, the IAM currently renders its local login page on /authorize even when it has a session. Use an upstream IdP for the zero-form path, or add an IAM session short-circuit.
Applications on the same TLD should use cookieDomain instead; it avoids the extra redirect and is simpler.
Complete example routes.json and README.md

body:
This example points Gate One straight at one OIDC issuer: no external IAM to federate, no embedded IAM. Gate One is the relying party; the issuer is the IdP and, because it also carries roles and scopes, the authorization source for that deployment.
A single Keycloak realm is used here, but the same shape works for any one issuer — Zitadel, Entra ID, Okta or Auth0.
Useful if you want to… authenticate users from exactly one identity provider;
use its roles, scopes and claims directly, with no extra service;
keep the Gate One configuration as small as possible.
If you must federate several IdPs, use an external IAM (Keycloak with Google) or the embedded IAM (Embedded IAM).
File examples/direct-oidc/routes.json
{ "authProvider": { "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com", "scopes": ["openid", "profile", "email"], "sessionKeyEnv": "OIDC_SESSION_KEY", "backchannelLogout": true }, "routes": [ { "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }, { "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/admin/*", "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": { "identity": { "roles": ["app-admin"] } } } ] } Why direct, and what you give up No claim mapping. Gate One’s default roleClaims and scopesClaim are Keycloak-shaped, so realm_access.roles, resource_access.<clientId>.roles, groups and scope are read with no configuration.
One provider, one session, no IAM, no federation. The file above is the whole authentication setup.
You reuse the IAM you already run — user lifecycle, groups, client scopes, audience mappers (for MCP), back-channel logout.
What you give up is federating several upstream IdPs behind one issuer; add that with an external IAM or the embedded IAM when you need it.
If your one provider is Google Google’s ID token carries possibly only an hd (hosted domain) claim, useful to restrict a route to your organization’s domain:
"auth": { "identity": { "claims": { "hd": "yourcompany.com" } } } If you need Google-issued tokens with roles, that is Google Cloud Identity Platform custom claims; otherwise put an IAM (Keycloak, Entra, Okta) or the embedded IAM in front of Google.
Run it The packaged demo runs Gate One against a local OIDC provider (Docker Compose):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/direct-oidc BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/direct-oidc](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/direct-oidc) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Register https://login.example.com/auth/callback at the issuer.
See also Multiple identity providers
Keycloak with Google

IAM services cover authorization and configure the identity providers (IdPs) they trust. Gate One sits between the user, an IAM/authorization source and an IdP. The schema’s authProvider.type is a provider type: it selects who Gate One asks to verify a request and obtain identity/authorization claims. It is not an IAM by itself. auth.identity is where Gate One enforces route policy. An IdP that also carries roles, scopes and claims is acting as the IAM for that deployment; Gate One still does not store users or assign rights. The three roles Role Question it answers Examples IAM / authorization What is this account allowed to do? Which tenants, roles, audiences and token lifetimes apply? cladone-auth, Keycloak, Entra ID, Auth0, Okta IdP / identification Who is this human? Google, Microsoft, Keycloak as an upstream IdP, a corporate LDAP/SAML directory Gate One / enforcement Is this request authenticated, and does it satisfy the route policy? authProvider, auth.identity, MCP scope checks An IAM can also be an IdP: Keycloak, Entra ID and Auth0 all do both. Gate One connects to the IAM, and the IAM configures the IdPs it trusts. Who configures whom flowchart TB ADMIN["Platform admin"] -->|"tenants, roles, audiences"| IAM["IAM / authorization

authProvider + route policy"] -->|"oidc: issuer + JWKS"| IAM GO -.->|"oidc direct: issuer + JWKS"| IDPS GO -->|"jwt: bearer + JWKS"| API["API / MCP issuer"] IAM -->|"token with roles+scopes+claims"| GO IDPS -.->|"roles, scopes, claims when provided"| GO GO -->|"verified identity + policy"| APP["Application"] Two valid shapes: With a separate IAM (recommended for several IdPs). The IAM owns the upstream IdP configuration (tenants[].upstreams), local policy, user grants and token issuance. Gate One points at the IAM with one oidc provider. Without a separate IAM. Gate One points directly at one OIDC provider that acts as both the IdP and the IAM/authorization server. It authenticates the user and emits the roles, scopes and claims Gate One enforces. This is simpler, but the provider must supply the claims your routes need. See the Direct OIDC example. In both shapes, Gate One enforces auth.identity per route; the IAM does not decide which application route a user may call. An IdP that only authenticates (for example a plain Google login) does not provide application roles; use an IAM or another claim source if you need them. New configurations should use http-bridge. oidc Gate One is the OpenID Connect relying party: discovery, authorization code + PKCE, state/nonce, JWKS, signed session, RP-initiated and back-channel logout. It hosts the login surface on loginBaseUrl. Use it for a direct OIDC IdP or for a cladone-auth tenant. This is the only provider type that combines a browser session with local revocation state (bbolt or Redis). The OIDC client must register every application origin as a valid post-logout redirect URI, or the IdP rejects the logout and its SSO session survives — see link:/docs/features/sso-multi-apps/#logout[Logout and revocation]. jwt Gate One validates a bearer token against a JWKS. It never hosts a login page and never issues a token. Use it for APIs and MCP clients, not for a browser session. http-bridge Gate One delegates verification to an HTTP service that implements the Gate One HTTP bridge contract. The bridge is where non-OIDC technologies are adapted: SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys, a legacy session service, or auth-bridge in front of Keycloak. Gate One only calls /auth, /auth/mcp and /health, and redirects the browser to the bridge’s login page. The bridge owns the protocol and, usually, the session cookie. See the HTTP bridge contract for endpoints, headers and status codes. IAM, bridge and token broker These names are easy to confuse: Name What it is Gate One talks to it via cladone-auth IAM Optional embedded IAM and OIDC issuer: IdP federation, users, claims, grants and tokens authProvider.type: "oidc" http-bridge Provider type for a service that verifies requests and returns identity/IAM facts authProvider.type: "http-bridge" auth-bridge Reference implementation of the http-bridge contract, often in front of Keycloak authProvider.type: "http-bridge" tokenBroker Internal per-user credential service used by upstream.tokenBroker Internal API, not an authProvider The IAM does not implement the HTTP bridge contract. It speaks OIDC and issues tokens; Gate One is the OIDC relying party. The bridge contract is a request-verification contract and the bridge owns the session for that provider type. See Embedded IAM for the IAM, Delegated credentials and Token broker for the per-user credential service, and HTTP bridge contract for the bridge. dev The embedded provider exists for onboarding and tests. It is loopback only, has real alice/bob accounts, and must not be exposed to a network. Internal OAuth IAM: cladone-auth cladone-auth is the optional internal OAuth/OIDC IAM. It is a small multi-tenant issuer with an IAM-side user directory: it federates external IdPs (Google, Microsoft, Keycloak, …) configured per tenant under tenants[].upstreams; it applies local policy: tenant, roles, audiences, allowed domains, admin emails, claim mappings and user grants; it stores one external identity link (issuer, subject) per federated user; it never recreates the IdP account; local and federated users both carry roles/scopes/claims, managed by the admin CLI; it emits its own Ed25519-signed ID/access/refresh tokens and publishes JWKS and discovery; it publishes the revocation keyspace Gate One reads for a global logout. It is deliberately lighter than Keycloak: one Go binary, one JSON file, Redis optional for multi-instance state, no realm/theme/admin console to operate. That makes it a good fit when you need several IdPs, normalized rights or local policy, but do not need a full IAM suite. flowchart LR GO["Gate One
authProvider + route policy"] -->|"authorize + token"| IAM["cladone-auth
tenant company"] IAM -->|"upstream login"| G["Google"] IAM -->|"upstream login"| M["Microsoft"] IAM -.->|"optional local password"| L["Local account

local + federated grants"] --- IAM MAPPINGS["claim mappings
IdP claims -> roles/scopes/claims"] --- IAM The recommended path is external IdPs: there is no password store to protect and no password-hash cost at login. Local accounts (localAccounts) are optional for small deployments; they use PBKDF2 and add the operational burden of a credential store. Claim mappings are evaluated on every federated login. Per-user grants are applied to both local and federated users, and changes take effect at the next login. Configuration: Embedded IAM feature Embedded IAM example Embedded IAM configuration reference cladone-auth vs auth-bridge Both can serve the same users, but they sit on opposite sides of OIDC: cladone-auth is an OIDC issuer and IAM. It federates upstream IdPs, holds the user directory, applies claim→rights policy and issues its own tokens. Gate One is the relying party (type: "oidc"). auth-bridge is an OIDC relying party and bridge. It runs the OIDC flow against Keycloak and answers Gate One with identity headers per the bridge contract (type: "http-bridge"). It does not issue tokens. Gate One injects the per-user token on upstream.tokenBroker routes and serves its browser routes (tokenBroker.browserHost) for either provider. It is therefore not a reason to choose one over the other — see Delegated credentials. body:
Gate One is a reverse proxy at the edge. It authenticates the request, applies route policy, optionally injects UX, then forwards the request to the existing application. The application keeps its own URL, stack and deployment; it does not need an SDK.
Request path flowchart TB C["Browser / API client"] --> G subgraph G["Gate One"] direction TB M["1. match route
host + path"] --> D["2. reserve durable
event space"] D --> A["3. authenticate
+ identity policy"] A --> T["4. verify anti-robot
token (Turnstile)"] T --> F["5. proxy, or
401 / 403 / 502 / 503"] F --> E["6. emit subscribed
event after the response"] end G -->|"OIDC / JWT"| I["Identity provider
or IAM"] G -->|"proxied request"| AP["Existing application"] G -.->|"HTTP/JSON event"| P["Out-of-process plugin"] The gateway does six things in order:
match the route by host and path;
reserve durable event space (when a durable type is subscribed);
authenticate and check the identity policy;
verify the anti-robot token on a protected form POST (Turnstile);
forward the request, or answer 401/403/502/503 itself;
emit the subscribed event after the response.
A failure at step 2 is a 503 before authentication, so an event the operator declared durable is not lost. A failure at step 3 never reaches the backend. A failed anti-robot check (step 4) is a 403 after the rate limit and before the backend; a Siteverify outage is a 503 — never a "you are a bot" answer.
Bot protection Cloudflare Turnstile is configured once, at the top level, and applies to every matching host/path. In forms mode Gate One injects the widget into matching forms and verifies the POST with Siteverify before the backend. In gate mode the first request to a protected path gets a challenge page at its own URL; solving it sets a signed 30-minute clearance cookie (HMAC, checked locally), and the following requests pass without another Siteverify call. both combines the two. It only covers traffic that passes through this instance: a second ingress or a published port bypasses it, so restrict the application’s network access to Gate One. See Turnstile.
Why run behind a reverse proxy Gate One protects applications as a reverse proxy, but it should itself sit behind a front reverse proxy or ingress controller in most deployments. The gateway listens on plain HTTP, so the ingress terminates TLS, publishes one stable public URL, load-balances and health-checks the replicas, and keeps WAF, rate limits and access logs in front. Gate One trusts X-Forwarded-* from that immediate hop and must not be reachable directly by clients.
See Reverse proxy for the forwarded headers and probes.
Provider types Mode Use External dependency dev
Onboarding, tests, local demos. A dedicated login.<domain> host, real alice/bob form, loopback only.
none
http-bridge
Any service implementing the Gate One HTTP bridge contract; auth-bridge is the reference. The legacy http alias is accepted.
auth-bridge or a custom bridge
oidc
Native OpenID Connect relying party: discovery, code + PKCE, state/nonce, JWKS, signed session, RP-initiated and back-channel logout, MCP bearer validation.
an OIDC Identity Provider (IdP) or IAM
jwt
Stateless JWKS bearer validation for APIs and MCP. No login page, no session cookie.
a JWT issuer with JWKS
authProvider is the single-provider form. authProviders
defaultAuthProvider + auth.provider bind one provider per route for multi-tenant hosting. Only oidc and jwt are allowed in the plural form; http-bridge and dev remain single-provider types.
For unrelated domains (for example app-a.com and app-b.fr), use ssoGroups: the shared OIDC/client/session settings are written once, providers[] declares one domain-specific provider, and routes[].hosts[] expands one route body across those domains. Each domain keeps its own Gate One cookie; the IdP session provides the zero-form login. This is not a shared cross-TLD cookie. See Cross-domain SSO.
An authentication provider is not a plugin. authProvider.type: "plugin" is rejected. Authentication adapters live in the embedded IAM and remain under the Gate One licence.
With or without the embedded IAM The embedded IAM is optional.
Without the embedded IAM, Gate One talks directly to one OIDC or JWT issuer per provider. This is the simplest production setup.
With the embedded IAM (cladone-auth), Gate One trusts one local issuer that federates Google, Microsoft, Auth0, Keycloak or local accounts, applies tenant policy and re-emits Ed25519-signed tokens. Gate One never trusts the upstream token.
The embedded IAM adds a second service and a second session (browser SSO on the IAM host), but it keeps the trust boundary local and makes multi-provider and multi-tenant setups uniform. It also publishes the revocation keyspace Gate One reads for a global logout.
Identity and injectable UX After authentication, Gate One knows an identity: user, roles, scopes, claims and an opaque subject id. It can:
enforce route conditions (auth.when, auth.identity);
add the opaque X-Gate-One-Subject header for the backend;
inject a user badge, a login guard, gated controls, a forbidden banner, a PWA shell and custom HTML/JS/CSS;
emit a strict CSP in merge, hash or nonce mode.
The injected guard is class-based and runs after the gateway has decided authentication. It is a UX layer, not an authorization boundary: hiding a control does not grant or revoke rights.
The authorization check itself is a first-class route setting. Configure auth.identity with the roles, scopes, claims or user that your backend expects, and Gate One returns 403 before forwarding a request that lacks them; MCP services get the equivalent scope check. This covers route-level rights validation. The backend still enforces its own resource-level permissions, because only it knows what a given record or action means.
Usage bus and plugins Usage events are opt-in per type. A plugin declares a subscription in a signed manifest; only then are those events produced.
one WAL per (node, type);
one cursor per (type, subscriber);
a node budget split into per-type shares;
fsync: always = zero loss before the response;
window_ms = group commit;
none = best effort;
onMaxLag: block = targeted 503 until the plugin catches up;
onMaxLag: drop = cursor advances to the lag limit and the plugin is marked degraded.
Events contain no token, cookie, email or username. The user is an opaque subjectId = v1. + HMAC(issuer, sub). The HMAC secret is held by the producer only.
Extensions are out-of-process HTTP/JSON services, verified by an Ed25519 manifest and a local trust store. There is no compile-time plugin API. See Plugins and the manifest reference.
Deployment and high availability A production deployment looks like this:
flowchart TB LB["Load balancer / ingress
TLS termination"] --> R1["Gate One
replica 1"] LB --> R2["Gate One
replica 2"] R1 --> RS[("Redis Sentinel
sessions + revocation")] R2 --> RS R1 --> AP["Existing application"] R2 --> AP Two replicas behind a load balancer; no published container port.
Shared state in Redis (Sentinel + TLS + ACL) with a versioned key prefix. A local bbolt file is valid for a single instance only. See Redis.
Same session key on every replica (sessionKeyEnv), and one shared ssoGroups session store for cross-TLD providers.
Health probes: /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness, including providers and usage).
Manual rolling restart: one replica at a time, 30-second stop grace, in-flight drain. There is no blue/green deployment yet.
WAL per node: a plugin consumes each node’s WAL.
Configuration reload: SIGHUP re-reads and validates the file, then swaps the gateway atomically. An invalid file is refused and the previous configuration stays active.
Fail closed: Redis unavailable on an authenticated route → 502 authentication_unavailable; a full durable share → targeted 503 usage_unavailable; a failed login audit → no session.
The Horizontal scaling feature and the High Availability example cover when to scale and the Redis-backed configuration.
What Gate One is not It is not an identity provider (the dev provider is for local development only).
It is not a token issuer; the embedded IAM is a separate optional service.
It is not a general-purpose authorization server: policy is per route (technical conditions, roles, scopes, claims), not per resource.
It is not a plugin runtime inside the request process: plugins never decide authentication and never sit on the hot path.
It does not provide commercial metering in the free/self-hosted edition; usage events are operational.

auth-bridge is the reference implementation of the HTTP bridge contract. Use it when your identity technology is not OAuth/OIDC — SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys, a legacy session service — or when you already run auth-bridge in front of Keycloak.
Gate One reaches it with authProvider.type: "http-bridge". The bridge owns the session; Gate One still enforces auth, auth.identity and MCP scope checks on every request.
Where the code lives The reference implementation is services/auth-bridge/ in the Gate One source repository, and it ships as services_<version>_src.tar.gz in each release. It is a small Node.js service with its own Dockerfile; it is not part of the gate-one binary.
Run it The bridge runs as its own container on the internal network. Build it and start it with its documented environment (see services/auth-bridge/README.md in the source repository):
docker build -t gate-one-auth-bridge services/auth-bridge docker run -d --name auth-bridge --network internal gate-one-auth-bridge Then point Gate One at it:
{ "authProvider": { "type": "http-bridge", "baseUrl": "http://auth-bridge:8080" } } A non-conforming service needs an adapter that implements the same endpoints; the contract is the specification.

This example starts from one protected application and adds a second route behind the same authentication provider. That is what creates SSO: the provider and the shared cookie domain are already in place, and the second route reuses the same Gate One session.
Changing the provider alone does not create SSO. Adding a route alone does not create SSO either. The two routes must use the same provider and share the same cookie domain.
File examples/sso-multi-apps/routes.json
{ "authProvider": { "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com" }, "routes": [ { "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }, { "host": "reports.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://reports:8080", "auth": {} } ] } The second reports.example.com route is the only addition needed for SSO, because it is under the same cookieDomain and uses the default provider.
Run it The packaged demo runs both applications and Gate One against a local OIDC provider (Docker Compose):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/sso-multi-apps BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/sso-multi-apps](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/sso-multi-apps) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Register https://login.example.com/auth/callback at the identity provider. Point DNS (or your test hosts file) for app.example.com, reports.example.com and login.example.com at Gate One.
What to observe Open https://app.example.com; log in.
Open https://reports.example.com in the same browser.
The second host must not redirect to the identity provider: the shared example.com session cookie is reused.
Why it works cookieDomain: "example.com" lets both hosts share the session cookie.
Both routes use the same authProvider and therefore the same issuer and session key.
This example runs a single Gate One instance, so the default bbolt session/revocation store is enough.
The second visit does not redirect to the identity provider.
Note The applications must share a parent domain. app.company.com and app.other.com cannot share a cookie.
On a single instance, a logout revokes the session for the next request. For several replicas, see High Availability.
The applications can stay public: remove "auth": {} from one route. Only that route becomes anonymous.
Next If you need several Gate One replicas, use High Availability. If your users come from several identity providers, see Keycloak with Google or Embedded IAM.

Useful if you want to… accept users from several identity providers (Google, Microsoft, GitHub, a corporate directory, …);
keep one issuer and one login surface for Gate One;
centralize user policy, roles and federation in an existing IAM;
avoid adding another identity service to the platform.
The classical pattern: an external IAM Usefull if you already use one
An OIDC IAM such as Keycloak or Zitadel can federate several IdPs itself. In that pattern:
users authenticate against the IAM;
the IAM delegates to Google, Microsoft or another upstream IdP;
the IAM applies users, groups, roles and policies;
Gate One points at one OIDC issuer — the IAM — and never sees the upstream IdPs.
browser -> Gate One -> Keycloak/Zitadel -> Google or another IdP Keycloak and Zitadel are common open-source choices. They already provide the IAM features you need: identity-provider federation, user directory, groups/roles, account management and an admin console.
The complete Gate One + Keycloak + Google setup is in the Keycloak with Google example.
The embedded alternative: cladone-auth If you do not want to run an external IAM, Gate One ships the optional embedded IAM cladone-auth. It is a lightweight OIDC issuer that:
federates external IdPs, so it is not an IdP itself;
keeps one login surface and one issuer for Gate One;
maps IdP IAM fields into a common roles/scopes/claims model;
manages per-user grants for both local and federated users.
It is deliberately resource-light: the recommended path uses external IdPs, so there is no password store and no password-hashing cost. Local accounts are optional for small deployments.
It is a lightweight IAM, not a full replacement for Keycloak/Zitadel: no per-resource policy engine, no admin UI, no multi-identity linking.
Feature: Embedded IAM
Example: Embedded IAM example
The simplest case: one IdP, direct OIDC If you have a single identity provider that already carries the roles and scopes your routes need, point Gate One straight at it: one oidc provider, no federation, no embedded IAM. See the Direct OIDC example.
Choosing If you… Use Already run Keycloak, Zitadel, Entra or Auth0
that IAM as the single OIDC issuer
Want federation without another IAM service
cladone-auth embedded IAM
Have only one IdP
direct oidc, no IAM needed (example)
Need full user lifecycle, admin console and enterprise policies
an external IAM such as Keycloak or Zitadel
In both patterns Gate One trusts one issuer and applies route policy locally; the difference is where user federation and administration live.
Important Gate One is not the IAM: it does not store users or assign rights.
With an external IAM, its roles/scopes must be present in the token claims configured for Gate One (roleClaims/scopesClaim).
With cladone-auth, the embedded IAM is an issuer and user directory, not a general per-resource policy engine.
Authentication adapters remain under the Gate One licence; they are not third-party extension plugins.

Gate One extensions are out-of-process services. They are trusted through a signed manifest and a local trust store; code is never loaded into the gateway. This page is the publisher/operator walkthrough: develop, sign, install and revoke.
Plugin families Extension families and what is not a plugin are defined once in Plugins. For publishers, the only fully signed extension today is the event consumer; injection bundles are route configuration and auth adapters stay in the IAM under the Gate One licence.
The trust model Three roles:
the plugin author writes the plugin;
the publisher holds a signing key and signs the manifest;
the operator runs Gate One and provisions the trust store.
The publisher signs the manifest once. The operator never re-signs: they only decide which keys and names they accept. The signature attests provenance and integrity — “this artefact is the one I signed and it is unchanged” — not quality.
Note Signing is not a quality gate. A valid signature says nothing about whether the plugin behaves. The lever that matters after deployment is revocation (see below): the publisher can withdraw trust once experience shows the plugin is wrong, on their own initiative or at the plugin author’s request (a bug, or a move to another model). Why it is useful: it enforces trust between parties. The operator trusts one publisher key instead of every developer; the publisher attests to what it signed; a swapped or tampered artefact fails closed (signature + digest); and revokedDigests gives recall.
Develop and test unsigned You do not need a signature to develop. Register the plugin with just name and url (plus types when there is no manifest):
"usage": { "dir": "./usage-wal", "subjectSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_SUBJECT_SECRET", "pluginSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET", "types": { "error": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "window_ms" } }, "plugins": [{ "name": "com.company.audit", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9100", "types": ["error"] }] } Gate One loads it and delivers events; nothing is verified. So a developer can iterate without a key pair.
Important An unsigned plugin is never silent. Gate One logs a CONFIG WARNING usage.plugins[<name>]: unsigned plugin (no manifest) at startup and in gate-one -check. The warning is for the operator only — end users are not shown plugin trust state, because they cannot act on it and it would leak deployment details.
Set usage.requireSigned: true in production: an unsigned plugin then becomes a hard load error instead of a warning.
Publish step by step (event consumer) Implement the service. It exposes GET /health and POST /events, and verifies the X-Gate-One-Assertion on every call (see the plugin contract).
Build the artefact and compute its sha256:<hex> digest (and optional size).
Write the manifest — name, version, hostAPI, artifact, capabilities: ["events"], and the events subscription.
Sign the manifest with the publisher key.
Distribute the artefact, the signed manifest and the public key.
The manifest { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "extension", "name": "com.company.audit", "version": "1.0.0", "apiVersion": "v1", "hostAPI": ">=1.0 <2.0", "keyId": "company-2026", "artifact": { "type": "binary", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 10485760, "platform": "linux/amd64" }, "capabilities": ["events"], "events": { "types": ["auth", "error"], "filters": { "statusClasses": ["4xx", "5xx"] }, "maxLagBytes": 5000000, "onMaxLag": "block" }, "signature": { "alg": "ed25519", "keyId": "company-2026", "value": "…" } } The manifest is authoritative for the subscription; the fields on the plugin entry (types, filters, maxLagBytes, onMaxLag) are used only when there is no manifest.
Signing the manifest The signature is Ed25519 over the JCS canonical form (RFC 8785) of the document with the signature member removed, followed by a newline and the artefact digest:
payload = JCS(manifest without the "signature" member) + "\n" + artifact.digest signature.value = base64url(ed25519_sign(private_key, payload)) JCS is a standard canonicalization (sorted keys, compact, defined number formatting), so any language with a JCS library can sign — the publisher does not have to be in Go.
The CLI does it for you:
# generate a key pair (Ed25519); prints the public key for the trust store gate-one keygen -out company-2026.json -keyId company-2026 # sign: fills artifact.digest/size and signature, writes the signed manifest gate-one sign -in manifest.json -key company-2026.json \ -artifact company-audit -out manifest.signed.json # also register it in a publisher feed (registry): author + distribution URL gate-one sign -in manifest.json -key company-2026.json \ -artifact company-audit -out manifest.signed.json \ --feed registry.json --publisher "Company Ltd" \ --distribution https://company.example/plugins/audit # check a signature (or a whole document) later gate-one verify -in manifest.signed.json -key company-2026.json -artifact company-audit The same gate-one sign/verify sign the publisher feed (a feed has no separate artefact, so no -artifact is passed). With --feed, sign also upserts this plugin into the feed and re-signs it, so a registry page can link the author and the distribution URL.
Distribute and advertise There is no Gate One-operated registry or marketplace today. Publishing is out-of-band, and the reverse-DNS name is the discovery key: an operator allow-lists it in trust-store.allowedNames (for example com.company.*) and registers the plugin in usage.plugins.
The publisher feed doubles as the registry. Each entry carries the plugin’s name, version, digest, publisher (author/company) and distribution URL, so it can be rendered as a page:
"plugins": [ { "name": "com.company.audit", "version": "1.0.0", "digest": "sha256:…", "publisher": "Company Ltd", "distribution": "https://company.example/plugins/audit", "status": "active" } ] Distribute the artefact + signed manifest + public key (and the SBOM) wherever you publish software — a release page, a package registry, a file share — and point distribution at it. The operator fetches from there, verifies against your key, and adds it to the trust store. The feed is also how you revoke and how operators learn which versions are compatible.
Trust lifecycle sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Dev as Plugin author participant Pub as Publisher (signer) participant Op as Operator participant GO as Gate One participant Pl as Plugin service Dev->>Pub: artefact + manifest draft + tests Pub->>Pub: sign manifest (Ed25519) Pub-->>Op: artefact + signed manifest + public key Op->>Op: trust store (key, allowedNames, allowedDependencies) Op->>GO: usage.plugins + usage.requireSigned GO->>GO: verify signature, digest, name, host API GO->>Pl: POST /events (signed assertion) Pl-->>GO: ack offsets Pub-->>Op: revoke (digest) if the plugin misbehaves Revocation Trust can be withdrawn after deployment. Three local mechanisms, applied by the operator (the trust store is provisioned out-of-band and never fetched from a plugin):
Revoke an artefact — add its sha256 digest to trust-store.revokedDigests. It is refused even with a valid signature.
Revoke a key — remove the key from trust-store.keys; everything that key signed is refused.
Reload — SIGHUP re-reads the trust store and the configuration; the next load of the plugin fails closed.
The publisher feed A revocation should not have to wait for every operator to edit a file. The publisher feed is a signed document the publisher maintains, listing the components that fit together and their revocation status:
{ "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "publisher-feed", "publisher": "Cladone-IT", "generatedAt": "2026-11-07T00:00:00Z", "validUntil": "2026-12-07T00:00:00Z", "hosts": [ { "name": "gate-one", "version": "1.5.0", "hostAPI": ">=1.0 <2.0" } ], "externalComponents": [ { "name": "redis", "role": "session-store", "constraint": ">=7.0 <8.0" } ], "plugins": [ { "name": "com.company.audit", "version": "1.0.0", "digest": "sha256:…", "publisher": "Company Ltd", "distribution": "https://company.example/plugins/audit", "status": "active" } ], "revocations": [ { "digest": "sha256:…", "reason": "misbehaviour", "severity": "high" } ], "signature": { "alg": "ed25519", "keyId": "cladone-2026", "value": "…" } } The operator points at it and pins the publisher key:
"publisherFeed": { "file": "publisher-feed.json", "keys": { "cladone-2026": "<base64 Ed25519 public key>" }, "mode": "enforce" } mode: warn (default) — revocations and incompatibilities are reported by gate-one -check and doctor; nothing is blocked.
mode: enforce — the feed’s revocations (by digest and by key) are merged into the plugin trust store, so a revoked plugin refuses to load; a plugin the feed marks revoked is refused when a digest is given. A stale (validUntil passed) feed refuses new loads rather than failing open.
The feed only narrows trust and advises (compatibility); the local trust store stays authoritative, and the operator can always override.
This is how the publisher — or the plugin author asking them — pulls a plugin out of production after experience shows it misbehaves, without waiting for a manual edit on every deployment.
Differences by plugin type Event consumer (events) — the implemented path; this page.
Injection / UI — today a per-route inject bundle (HTML/JS/CSS and client-side patches), referenced by route.inject and validated against inject-bundle.schema.json. It is a configuration file, not a signed plugin; a signed-bundle path is planned.
Auth adapter (kind: auth) — IAM-only and under the Gate One licence; it is not an extension and cannot be signed by a third party.
There is deliberately no “route handler” plugin: a Backend-For-Frontend is a proxied backend: route, and response transforms are the gateway’s native injector chain. Adding an out-of-process transform would buffer the response and sit on the hot path, which Gate One avoids.
Install on the operator side "usage": { "dir": "./usage-wal", "subjectSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_SUBJECT_SECRET", "pluginSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET", "trustStore": "trust-store.json", "requireSigned": true, "types": { "auth": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "always" } }, "plugins": [{ "name": "com.company.audit", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9100", "manifest": "company-audit.manifest.json", "artifact": "company-audit" }] } a signed manifest requires usage.trustStore;
artifact is the file whose digest the manifest signs (Gate One verifies it, it does not launch it — the service must be running at url);
relative paths are resolved from the configuration file;
instead of inline entries, usage.pluginsDir (conventionally plugins.d) scans every *.json descriptor in a directory; a descriptor has the same shape as one usage.plugins[] entry, and its manifest/artifact paths are relative to the descriptor;
SIGHUP reloads the configuration, including plugins.
The complete signed example is the usage-plugin example.

This guide is the contract for the declarative gating attributes read by the injected guard script. The behavioural matrix at the end is the one executed by test/ui/controls.mjs against the page fixture test/ui/controls.html.
Attributes Attribute Meaning data-gtw-auth="before"
The action is neutralised while anonymous: preventDefault()
stopPropagation(), then the login tab opens. Authenticate first, act after. Activation only: turning a feature OFF is a deactivation and is always let through without login.
data-gtw-auth="after"
The native action proceeds while anonymous; the login tab opens as an invitation. The 401 request produced by the action is queued and replayed after login. Activation only: a deactivation does not open the login tab.
data-gtw-auth-off="value"
For value controls (select, range, date, time, datetime-local, month, week, color): the value considered OFF. Moving to it is a deactivation (free); moving away from it is an activation. Default: the control’s default value (for a select: the option carrying selected, otherwise the first option). Ignored by the other control families.
data-gtw-auth-hidden="before"
Hidden while anonymous, shown once authenticated. Activating clicks are neutralised and show the sign-in banner; a checked checkbox may still be unchecked (deactivation).
data-gtw-auth-hidden="after"
Visible while anonymous, hidden once authenticated (pure affordance, composable with data-gtw-auth="before" for padlocks).
data-gtw-roles, data-gtw-scopes, data-gtw-claims
Identity-conditioned visibility, evaluated after the session probe.
data-gtw-logout
Wires the click to the OIDC logout navigation. Authenticated only.
Markup wins over the equivalent uiGate rule: an element carrying a data-gtw-auth (or data-gtw-auth-hidden) attribute is not affected by a config rule for the same dimension.
data-gtw-claims (and uiGate[].claims) takes a JSON object: each key must match, each value is one accepted string or a list of accepted strings (OR / anyOf on the same claim), and "*" means "claim present". A token claim that is itself a list (groups, token roles…) matches when one element matches. Example: data-gtw-claims='{"email": ["alice@example.com", "a.rolland@example.com"]}'.
Control families The guard distinguishes three kinds of interaction:
Family Controls Rule Click is the action
checkbox, radio, details/summary, aria-pressed/aria-checked/aria-expanded, reset, submit, button, file, links
Gated on click. The state read at click time decides activation vs deactivation.
Change is the action
select, range, date, time, datetime-local, month, week, color
The click only opens the picker and is never gated. The change event is gated, with data-gtw-auth-off (or the default value) as the OFF value.
Click is focus
text, search, email, url, tel, password, number, textarea
Never gated on click: the click only focuses the field. Put data-gtw-auth on the submit button instead.
Notes:
reset is always a deactivation: it never opens a login, even with data-gtw-auth. Use a normal button if the reset itself must be gated.
file is an activation: the picker is opened only after login. To allow choosing a file anonymously and gate the upload, put the attribute on the submit button.
A radio’s pre-click state is remembered on pointerdown/keydown; clicking the already-selected radio is a no-op and does not open the login. A synthesised click without those events is treated as an activation.
details uses open at click time: closed → opening is an activation; open → closing is a deactivation.
aria-* toggles use the attribute value at click time: "false" → activating; "true" → deactivating. The application toggles the attribute in its own click handler (which the guard lets run only when the action is allowed).
data-gtw-auth-off is read from the element, its gating ancestor or its label[for]; a value on the element overrides a value on the ancestor.
