uiGate equivalence A config rule {"selector": "…​", "auth": "before"|"after"} has the same semantics as data-gtw-auth, including the activation-only rule, the passive-control exemption and the change-based gating of value controls. For a value control the OFF value is the control’s default value; a data-gtw-auth-off attribute on the element overrides it.
A config rule {"selector": "…​", "hidden": "before"} keeps the hidden dimension: it neutralises activating clicks and shows the banner, but a deactivation of a checked checkbox is still free.
Limitations Single-select only: select multiple is not covered by the value-off comparison in this version.
input events are not gated: for range and date/time/color pickers, the guard reacts to change. An application that updates live on input sees the transient value before a before revert.
Programmatic checkbox/radio changes are invisible: setting el.checked = true fires no DOM event. The login is requested at the first real request (401 → banner) or explicitly by the application through window.__cladoneAuth.login().
Radio arrow-key selection is not click-gated: moving the selection with the arrow keys fires change without click. Clicking (or Space) is gated; arrow-key selection is left to the server-side auth.when policy. A dispatched change on a gated radio is also not reverted by the click-based state machine.
Ambiguous wrappers: with several controls under one gated wrapper, put data-gtw-auth on each control. The guard resolves the target’s own control when it can, otherwise the first match.
reset is always free: use a normal button to gate a reset.
file click is an activation: gate the submit button if the picker itself must stay available anonymously.
Running the tests cd test/ui npm install npm test # matrix + uiGate + controls + forbidden suites npm run preview # visual preview: http://127.0.0.1:8787/ node run.mjs --served # behavioural smoke against the deployed page The fixture page is test/ui/controls.html; the assertions are in test/ui/controls.mjs. The guard script is rendered from the source at every run, so a stale embedded script can never pass the suite.
Local visual preview npm run preview starts a small local server that injects the guard into controls.html and provides a demo auth-bridge:
http://127.0.0.1:8787/ — the controls page with the guard injected; each case is preceded by a label naming the element, the data-gtw-* attribute and the value exercised;
a gated control opens a login tab with a Sign in (demo) button; the demo session is stored in a cookie and the tab posts cladone-auth:ok back to the page;
Force authenticated, Reset demo session, and the user-card logout change the demo session in place: no redirect, no reload, so the page keeps its scroll position and the focused feature;
the user-card logout is a preview override of window.__cladoneAuth.logout(); production still performs the OIDC end_session navigation;
/?authed=1 and /logout remain available as manual shortcuts;
the toolbar shows the current state;
the badge is at the top right: approach the top edge (the toolbar reserves that corner and stays below the badge) to reveal it, then click it to unfold the claims and the logout button.
The preview is for visual inspection; the assertions remain in controls.mjs and are run by npm test.

Gate One runs from an offline signed licence: an Ed25519 token that the gateway verifies locally. It never calls home and needs no network. Without a valid token the gateway keeps serving in evaluation mode — a licence changes the badge and the host coverage, never the availability of the service.
One token per period A customer holds one token per purchased period. Install all of them:
/etc/gate-one/licences.d/ licence-2026-01-01-2027-01-01.txt 3 domains, 1 replica licence-2027-01-01-2028-01-01.txt 2 domains, 2 replicas The active periods are merged:
domains and features are unioned;
domainCount and maxReplicas take the maximum.
A renewal that reduces the domain count therefore never removes what the current period already paid for: the reduction applies when the new period starts.
Configuration { "license": { "tokenDir": "/etc/gate-one/licences.d", "publicKeys": { "2026-01": "<base64 Ed25519 public key>" }, "enforce": "info", "url": "https://licence.example.com" } } tokenDir — every regular file holds one token. Dropping a file and sending SIGHUP is enough; no restart.
publicKeys — kid to public key. Rotating a signing key adds an entry without invalidating the tokens already installed.
enforce — host coverage mode: info (default), warn, strict.
url — registration or renewal page linked from the badge.
tokenFile / token — single-token forms, kept for compatibility.
GATE_ONE_LICENSE_TOKEN adds one more token (the other sources stay active).
Domains and host coverage domains holds suffixes, not hosts. A suffix covers itself and every subdomain, so exemple.fr also covers app.exemple.fr and a.b.exemple.fr. Internal names work the same way: corp.local covers wiki.corp.local.
At load, the gateway collects every host it can serve — route host and hosts[], provider loginBaseUrl, cookieDomain, ssoGroups domains — and compares them with the active suffixes. localhost and loopback addresses are always allowed.
| enforce | Uncovered host | |---|---| | info (default) | logged, request served | | warn | logged as a warning, request served | | strict | 503 with license_uncovered_host |
Evaluation mode (no active token) is never blocked, in any mode: a future-only token, a missing directory or an expired licence does not take the deployment down.
What the badge shows The injected badge receives the licence state only: registered or evaluation, the expiry and the registration link. Company name, contact email, domains and features stay on the server — the guard script is embedded in every protected page, so anything sent to it is public.
Plugins Each plugin call carries X-Gate-One-License: the base64url-encoded licence view (state, enforce mode, domainCount, maxReplicas, domains, features). Its SHA-256 is bound into the signed X-Gate-One-Assertion, so a plugin can trust those facts. See the reference plugin (cmd/plugin-audit-echo) for the verification.

authProvider.type: "http-bridge" delegates request verification to an external HTTP service: the bridge. The bridge adapts a technology Gate One does not implement natively — SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys, a legacy session service — to three small endpoints and a login page.
Gate One never sees the upstream protocol. It only asks the bridge whether the request is authenticated and, for MCP, whether the token carries the required scope.
Important The bridge returns identity facts, not routing decisions. Gate One still enforces auth, auth.identity and MCP scope checks on every request. A bridge may return only X-User-Id, or also roles, scopes and claims. sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Browser participant G as Gate One participant Br as HTTP bridge participant I as SAML / LDAP / mTLS / API key B->>G: Request + cookies G->>Br: GET /auth with cookies and X-Forwarded-* Br->>I: protocol-specific verification I-->>Br: identity facts Br-->>G: 200 + X-User-* + Set-Cookie G-->>B: proxied response The legacy type http is an alias of http-bridge. The contract is the same; new configurations should use http-bridge.
Endpoints Method Path Purpose GET /auth Verify a browser/API request (cookies or Authorization) GET /auth/mcp Verify an MCP bearer token and its scope GET /health Readiness probe GET /login Browser login page (the URL Gate One redirects to) GET /logout Sign-out endpoint used by the injected user badge baseUrl is the bridge root. verifyUrl, mcpVerifyUrl, healthUrl and loginUrl can override the defaults (baseUrl + /auth, /auth/mcp, /health, /login).
Gate One redirects a browser navigation to:
{loginUrl}?returnTo={absolute-url-of-the-refused-request} The bridge must authenticate the user and then return the browser to returnTo. Do not put a query string in loginUrl itself: Gate One appends ?returnTo=... literally.
GET /auth Gate One sends the incoming request’s credentials to the bridge:
Request header Meaning Authorization Copied verbatim when the client sent one Cookie Every incoming cookie, verbatim X-Forwarded-Host Original host X-Forwarded-Uri Original URI including query X-Forwarded-Method Original method The bridge returns:
Status Meaning Gate One reaction 200 Authenticated Identity headers are read; Set-Cookie is relayed 401 / 403 Not authenticated ErrUnauthenticated; API gets 401, navigation redirects to login 3xx No session (auth-bridge redirects to /login) Same as unauthenticated 5xx / network error Bridge unavailable 502 authentication_unavailable; never a login redirect Identity response headers Defaults match auth-bridge; override them with authProvider.headers:
Header Default Content X-User-Id required Stable subject identifier X-Username optional Display/login name X-Email optional Email (used only for the badge/403 page) X-Roles optional Comma-separated roles X-Scopes optional Comma-separated scopes X-Claims optional Base64(standard) JSON object of additional claims Set-Cookie response headers are relayed to the browser verbatim: a bridge may refresh its session while verifying a request.
GET /auth/mcp Gate One sends the client Authorization header plus two internal headers it builds itself:
Header Meaning X-MCP-Scope Scope required by the MCP route X-MCP-Resource Protected-resource identifier/audience, when configured The bridge must ignore client-supplied values for these headers: only the values set by Gate One on the internal call are trusted.
Status Meaning 200 Token valid, scope satisfied; identity headers apply 401 Token missing/invalid 403 Token valid but insufficient scope Other Provider unavailable → 502 GET /health Any 2xx means ready. A non-2xx or a network error marks the provider unavailable. Gate One exposes /readyz accordingly and never redirects to a login page when the provider itself is down.
Cookies and session ownership For http-bridge, the bridge owns the session. Gate One does not create an RP session cookie and does not have a bbolt/Redis session store for this provider. It relays Set-Cookie and sends the browser’s cookies back on the next verification call.
As a consequence:
a global logout is the bridge’s responsibility; the injected user badge navigates to {loginUrl origin}/logout; the built-in identity-403 page has no automatic “sign out” link for this type (there is no Gate One RP session to clear). Minimal adapter sketch The bridge is deliberately small. A Python/Flask sketch for a legacy session service:
from flask import Flask, request, make_response import base64, json app = Flask(__name__) @app.get("/auth") def auth(): session = request.cookies.get("legacy_session") if not session or not legacy_sessions.valid(session): return "", 401 user = legacy_sessions.user(session) resp = make_response("", 200) resp.headers["X-User-Id"] = user.id resp.headers["X-Username"] = user.name resp.headers["X-Roles"] = ",".join(user.roles) resp.headers["X-Claims"] = base64.b64encode( json.dumps({"department": user.department}).encode() ).decode() return resp @app.get("/health") def health(): return {"status": "ok"} A complete example is examples/http-bridge/routes.json. Configure:
{ "authProvider": { "type": "http-bridge", "baseUrl": "http://legacy-bridge:8080", "loginUrl": "http://legacy-bridge:8080/login", "headers": { "userId": "X-User-Id", "username": "X-Username", "roles": "X-Roles", "claims": "X-Claims" } }, "routes": [{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } Security requirements Run the bridge on an internal network; never expose it through the public ingress. Gate One is its only client. Do not trust X-Forwarded-* from an external client; Gate One sets them on the internal call, but a publicly reachable bridge would let an attacker forge them. Validate cookies/tokens with the upstream technology; never return identity headers for an unauthenticated request. Return 5xx only for bridge/upstream outages; use 401/403 for credential and scope failures so Gate One does not turn an outage into a login loop. Keep X-MCP-Scope / X-MCP-Resource handling internal: Gate One overwrites them on the outbound call, but the bridge must not accept them from an arbitrary client. What the contract is not It is not an OIDC/OAuth discovery endpoint: use type: "oidc" for that. It is not implemented by the cladone-auth IAM. The IAM is an OIDC issuer/IAM and Gate One connects to it with type: "oidc"; it does not expose /auth, /auth/mcp or /health. auth-bridge is the reference implementation of this request-verification contract; its source is services/auth-bridge in the Gate One source repository. It is not the tokenBroker block. That service supplies per-user upstream credentials for upstream.tokenBroker; it is unrelated to authentication provider selection.

This example puts two unrelated domains behind one IdP session. Each domain keeps its own Gate One cookie; no cookie crosses the TLD boundary.
Files examples/cross-tld-sso/routes.json
examples/cross-tld-sso/README.md
Shared group, per-domain providers { "ssoGroups": [{ "id": "company", "issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "sessionKeyEnv": "OIDC_SESSION_KEY", "sessionStore": { "type": "redis", "url": "redis://redis:6379/0", "prefix": "cladone:auth:v1:" }, "providers": [ { "id": "app-a", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.app-a.com", "cookieDomain": "app-a.com", "defaultAppUrl": "https://app-a.com/" }, { "id": "app-b", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.app-b.fr", "cookieDomain": "app-b.fr", "defaultAppUrl": "https://app-b.fr/" } ] }], "defaultAuthProvider": "app-a", "routes": [{ "hosts": ["app-a.com", "app-b.fr"], "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } issuer, clientId, sessionStore and sessionKeyEnv are written once. Each provider entry only carries its domain, login host and optional cookie name. The route is written once; Gate One expands it to app-a.com and app-b.fr and binds each one to its provider.
Run it The packaged demo runs two Gate One instances and Redis; it is the same shared-state shape (Docker Compose):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/redis BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/redis](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/redis) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... export OIDC_SESSION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" export REDIS_PASSWORD=... gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Register both callbacks at the IdP:
https://login.app-a.com/auth/callback
https://login.app-b.fr/auth/callback
What to verify Log in on app-a.com once.
Visit app-b.fr with the same browser. Gate One redirects to the same IdP and returns without a login form.
Log out on app-a.com; the next request on app-b.fr must be refused (back-channel logout or shared Redis revocation).
Expire/clear the IdP session; the next visit must show the normal login form, not a loop.
Note This is zero form, not zero redirect.
Both domains must use the same issuer and the same user identity.
Use cookieDomain instead when the applications share a parent domain.

This example uses Keycloak as the IAM and OIDC issuer, with Google as an additional identity provider inside Keycloak. Gate One only sees the Keycloak issuer; it does not configure Google directly.
browser -> Gate One -> Keycloak -> Google File examples/keycloak-google/routes.json
{ "authProvider": { "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com", "roleClaims": ["realm_access.roles", "groups"] }, "routes": [{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } Keycloak setup Create the realm company.
Create an OIDC client gate-one:
Valid redirect URIs: https://login.example.com/auth/callback;
Valid post logout redirect URIs: https://app.example.com/* — one entry per application host (the host Gate One sends as post_logout_redirect_uri).
Add an Identity Provider of type Google and enter the Google client ID/secret. Complete the Google OAuth consent configuration.
Add a mapper/claim so Keycloak roles or groups appear in the token (realm_access.roles is included by default; groups requires a group-membership mapper).
Optionally add a role mapper to expose application roles as roles.
Gate One does not need the Google client ID or secret. Those stay in Keycloak.
Important Register a post logout redirect URI for every application host. Gate One’s logout sends the originating application as post_logout_redirect_uri; an unregistered host makes Keycloak answer Invalid redirect uri and, crucially, does not end the Keycloak SSO session — the user is then signed back in silently on the next visit. See Logout and revocation.
Run it export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Register https://login.example.com/auth/callback as the Keycloak client redirect URI, and https://app.example.com/* as a valid post logout redirect URI. Point app.example.com, login.example.com and auth.example.com at the right hosts.
What to observe Gate One redirects to Keycloak, and Keycloak offers Google (or another configured IdP) on its login page.
The Gate One session is created from the Keycloak issuer, not from Google.
roleClaims maps Keycloak roles/groups into Gate One’s route policy.
Note Google must be configured and tested in Keycloak first; Gate One cannot diagnose the upstream Google configuration.
Keycloak is now the IAM: user policy, groups and IdP federation live there.
If you do not want to run Keycloak, see Embedded IAM.
Next See Multiple identity providers for the pattern and the embedded alternative.

Useful if you want to… expose an API only to authenticated users, with roles, scopes or claim conditions per route;
accept machine clients with a bearer JWT, validated locally against a JWKS;
expose MCP tools with the OAuth protected-resource metadata clients expect (resource/audience, scope, tool list);
keep the browser session and the machine token planes separate.
Two planes Browser session. Gate One hosts (or delegates) the login page, sets an RP session cookie and proxies the request after authentication. Use type: "oidc" (or http-bridge for auth-bridge).
Machine bearer. A client presents Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. Gate One validates the signature through the provider’s JWKS, then the audience and the identity conditions. Use type: "jwt"; this provider never hosts a login page and never issues a token.
Route rules auth.when decides when authentication is required from technical conditions (method, query, header, body). auth.identity decides who is allowed after a successful authentication:
{ "host": "api.example.com", "path": "/v1/*", "backend": "http://api:8080", "auth": { "provider": "company-api", "when": { "method": ["GET", "POST"] }, "identity": { "scopes": ["read:things"], "roles": ["user"] } } } An empty auth ({}) means authentication is always required.
A claim condition accepts one value or a list: the listed values are OR-ed (anyOf) on the same claim, while distinct keys still combine with AND. Array-valued token claims (groups, token roles…) match when one element matches.
"identity": { "claims": { "email": ["alice@example.com", "a.rolland@example.com"], "email_verified": "true" } } JWT provider { "id": "company-api", "type": "jwt", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/t/company", "jwksUrl": "https://auth.example.com/t/company/jwks.json", "audience": "https://api.example.com" } issuer is advertised in metadata; jwksUrl is required; audience is checked when non-empty. The JWKS is cached (cacheTtlSeconds) and refreshed on an unknown key.
MCP An MCP route declares its protected-resource identity:
{ "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/mcp", "backend": "http://mcp:8080", "auth": { "provider": "company-api" }, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "path": "/mcp", "name": "things", "resource": "https://mcp.example.com", "scope": "mcp-tools", "operations": [ { "name": "list_things", "operationId": "listThings" } ] } } Gate One then serves:
/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource metadata for the endpoint;
authorization checks against the bearer token’s scope and aud;
the declared REST operations as MCP tools;
optional grouping of several services under one endpoint with mcpSets (the set carries the audience, scope and identity).
An external MCP server can also be proxied with mcp.upstream.url instead of declared operations.
This article covers the protection. How the tool list is built — deriving tools from an OpenAPI document, proxying an MCP server, aggregating with mcpSets — is in MCP tools.
An MCP tool that must call an external API as the user (GitHub, GitLab, …) uses delegated credentials: upstream.tokenBroker injects the caller’s per-user token from the token broker into every tool call. See Delegated credentials.
Complete example examples/protect-api-mcp/routes.json shows one browser provider, one JWT provider, an API route with an identity condition and an MCP service.
Operational notes A jwt provider is stateless: no cookie, no session store, no login host. It is the right choice for machine-to-machine and MCP clients.
auth.when is evaluated before authentication; it cannot inspect the identity. Use auth.identity for roles/scopes/claims.
The MCP audience check fails closed. If the issuer does not put the resource in aud, configure an audience mapper or use mcpAudience: "auto" with an issuer that supports it.
Token issuance, refresh and client registration are the issuer’s job; Gate One only validates.
Configuration reference routes[.auth]
routes[.auth.identity]
routes[.mcp]
mcpSets

This example runs the optional embedded IAM cladone-auth as the single OIDC issuer for Gate One. cladone-auth federates one or more upstream IdPs (Google, Microsoft Entra, Auth0, any OIDC issuer — each keyed under upstreams) and normalizes their claims into the roles/scopes/claims Gate One enforces. Files examples/embedded-iam/embedded-iam.json examples/embedded-iam/routes.json Embedded IAM configuration { "publicUrl": "https://auth.example.com", "listen": ":8081", "redis": { "url": "redis://redis:6379/0", "passwordEnv": "REDIS_PASSWORD", "prefix": "cladone:iam:v1:", "authPrefix": "cladone:auth:v1:" }, "tenants": [{ "id": "company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "MYCOMPANY_IAM_CLIENT_SECRET", "redirectUris": ["https://login.example.com/auth/callback"], "postLogoutRedirectUris": ["https://app.example.com/"], "upstreams": { "google": { "issuer": "https://accounts.google.com", "clientIdEnv": "GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID", "clientSecretEnv": "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET", "hostedDomain": "example.com" }, "microsoft": { "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/v2.0", "clientIdEnv": "MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID", "clientSecretEnv": "MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET", "optional": true } }, "defaultRoles": ["user"], "allowedDomains": ["example.com"], "mappings": [ { "claim": "groups", "values": ["admins"], "roles": ["admin"] } ], "rules": [ { "when": [{ "claim": "email", "match": "domain", "values": ["example.com"] }], "then": { "roles": ["employee"], "copyClaims": [ { "from": "email", "to": "email_domain", "transforms": ["keep:@:-1", "lower"] } ] } }, { "when": [{ "claim": "groups", "match": "glob", "values": ["team-*"] }], "then": { "rolesFrom": [ { "claim": "groups", "transforms": ["keep:-:-1", "lower"] } ] } } ] }] } upstreams is a map keyed by IdP id; each key is the value of the idp authorize parameter and the label on the built-in IdP chooser. An optional upstream is skipped (not shown, not validated) until its credentials exist, so you can ship it ahead of the secrets. mappings translates IdP-specific claims into the common model (the legacy groupRoles block is still accepted for the groups claim). rules is the richer when/then policy — see below. Gate One configuration { "authProviders": [{ "id": "company", "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/t/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "MYCOMPANY_OIDC_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com", "roleClaims": ["roles"], "sessionKeyEnv": "MYCOMPANY_SESSION_KEY", "sessionStore": { "type": "redis", "url": "redis://redis:6379/0", "passwordEnv": "REDIS_PASSWORD", "prefix": "cladone:auth:v1:" } }], "defaultAuthProvider": "company", "routes": [{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": { "provider": "company" } }] } The Redis store is here because this example is also the multi-instance form; a single IAM instance can use its memory store, and a single Gate One instance can use the default bbolt store. The tenant’s postLogoutRedirectUris lists where a logout may return. List every application origin (here app.example.com); an empty list falls back to redirectUris, which covers only the login host, so a logout from an application host would be refused. See Logout and revocation. Dynamic rights (rules) Federated users are created at first login with no rights (JIT). Two additive mechanisms grant rights: rules — evaluated on every login against the incoming token’s claims; the result is never persisted on the user. This is how you give a group of users (by email, domain, subject or IdP group) the right roles/scopes/claims automatically. cladone-auth user set — a persisted per-user exception (below). A rule reads the token (when) and writes the user (then): { "when": [ { "claim": "email", "match": "domain", "values": ["example.com"] }, { "claim": "groups", "values": ["support"] } ], "then": { "roles": ["employee"], "scopes": ["read:things"], "claims": { "department": "support" }, "rolesFrom": [{ "claim": "groups", "transforms": ["keep:-:-1", "lower"] }], "copyClaims": [{ "from": "email", "to": "email_domain", "transforms": ["keep:@:-1", "lower"] }] } } when — the test, evaluated against the incoming token. Each condition names a claim and either matches values (match: exact (default), prefix, suffix, domain, glob) or just requires the claim to be present. Several conditions are combined with AND. then.roles / scopes / claims — constant grants: applied whenever the test passes, regardless of which value matched. then.rolesFrom — derived roles: each value of the claim becomes a role. then.copyClaims — derived claims: copy an incoming claim into the issued token, optionally renamed (to) and reshaped. transforms is an ordered pipeline applied to every value: lower, upper, prefix:

, suffix:

, replace::, and keep::[:] — keep the fields from..to (negative counts from the end) joined by ; a single index keeps one field. So keep:@:-1 is the email domain, keep:@:0 the local part, keep:@:0:-2 drops the last field (a@b@c → a@b), and keep:-:-1 turns team-support into support. Reserved claims (iss, sub, aud, roles, scope, email, …) can never be written. Before the first login (pre-provisioning) A federated user has no IAM record until the first login (JIT). To give rights to someone who has never signed in, put the condition in a rule: it is evaluated at each login, so the rights are already there the first time — without creating a user in advance. By email when.claim: "email" accepts one value or a list. With match: "exact" (the default), the list is effectively a group of emails: "rules": [{ "when": [{ "claim": "email", "match": "exact", "values": ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"] }], "then": { "roles": ["support"], "scopes": ["read:things"] } }] When Alice or Bob signs in for the first time, the IAM creates the user and issues the support role and the read:things scope. For a whole domain or team, use domain, suffix or glob: "rules": [ { "when": [{ "claim": "email", "match": "domain", "values": ["example.com"] }], "then": { "roles": ["employee"] } }, { "when": [{ "claim": "email", "match": "glob", "values": ["*@team.example.com"] }], "then": { "roles": ["contractor"] } } ] exact is case-sensitive; domain, prefix, suffix and glob are case-insensitive. Lowercase the addresses in the configuration (or use glob) if the IdP does not guarantee the case. By upstream group (recommended) The cleanest "group → role" is the group managed by the IdP (Google Workspace, Entra, Keycloak…): the groups claim is mapped at login. "mappings": [ { "claim": "groups", "values": ["support"], "roles": ["support"] }, { "claim": "groups", "values": ["finance"], "roles": ["finance"] } ] or with the richer rule engine: "rules": [{ "when": [{ "claim": "groups", "values": ["support"] }], "then": { "roles": ["support"], "claims": { "department": "support" } } }] Membership is maintained in the IdP: removing the user from the group removes the role at the next login. What is evaluated at login first login -> JIT user (issuer, subject, email) -> defaultRoles -> mappings / legacy groupRoles (upstream claims) -> rules (email, domain, groups, sub, custom claims) -> persisted grants (user set; the user must already exist) Approach Named group? Lifecycle rules + email list the list is the group static; edit the config, reload rules + domain/glob no static IdP group (groups claim) yes, managed in the IdP automatic at the next login AdminEmails no (admin only) static, case-insensitive email list user set -issuer/-sub no (persisted exception) requires the user to exist AdminEmails is the built-in email list that grants admin to those addresses; it is the only email-to-role shortcut outside the rules. A rule result is never persisted on the user: it is recomputed at each login. Removing an address from the list (or the user from the IdP group) removes the role at the next login, but the JIT account remains with any persisted grants. To remove the account itself, use cladone-auth user delete once the user has signed in at least once. user set needs an existing user (issuer/sub), so it cannot pre-provision a federated identity. For a local account, create it explicitly with its rights — it is a local identity, not the federated one: cladone-auth user create -config embedded-iam.json -tenant company \ -kind local -email alice@example.com -password '...' \ -roles support The email claim must be present in the upstream token: the default scopes include email. If the IdP does not expose it, use groups or sub as the rule condition instead. Users and grants The rules above cover the common case. For a one-off exception, assign roles/scopes/claims to a specific user (persisted): # inspect the JIT user (issuer/subject come from the IdP token) cladone-auth user list -config embedded-iam.json -tenant company cladone-auth user show -config embedded-iam.json -tenant company \ -issuer https://accounts.google.com -sub 'google-sub-1' # assign common rights cladone-auth user set -config embedded-iam.json -tenant company \ -issuer https://accounts.google.com -sub 'google-sub-1' \ -roles support -scopes read:things \ -claims '{"department":"support"}' Local users use the same commands with -kind local and a password. The same roles/scopes/claims model applies to both. If the IdP subject changes unexpectedly, relink the same IAM user with -new-issuer/-new-sub instead of deleting it; its grants are preserved. Run it The packaged demo runs Gate One, cladone-auth, a local OIDC provider and Redis (Docker Compose): cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/embedded-iam BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/embedded-iam](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/embedded-iam) for the stack and its README. To run it by hand instead: # embedded IAM export REDIS_PASSWORD=... export MYCOMPANY_IAM_CLIENT_SECRET=... export GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=... GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=... cladone-auth -config embedded-iam.json # gate one export MYCOMPANY_OIDC_SECRET=... export MYCOMPANY_SESSION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json What to observe the IAM’s IdP chooser, then Google login; the IAM session cookie on auth.example.com; roleClaims: ["roles"] and the mapped admin role in the Gate One policy; cladone-auth user show after first login, then a grant update that appears on the next login; a global logout revoking sid and sub. Note The IAM is an issuer and user directory, not a per-resource policy engine; route rules stay in Gate One. One external identity link per user; no account linking. Upstream secrets stay in environment variables. If you already run Keycloak/Zitadel, use them as the external IAM: Keycloak with Google.

The token broker is the optional companion service behind Delegated credentials. It holds a registry of OAuth 2.0 providers and an encrypted per-user token store, and hands Gate One the access token of one authenticated user for one provider.
It is deliberately not an identity provider and not a reverse proxy: Gate One keeps its own identity; the broker only obtains and stores the user’s token for an upstream service.
Pause, resume and erase Disconnect is a pause, not a deletion. The credential stays stored and Connect resumes the same delegation; the provider is never contacted by pause or erase.
Action Effect Provider called? Connect
starts the OAuth flow when nothing is stored, or resumes a paused delegation with the stored token (refresh if needed; OAuth if the token can no longer work)
on a new authorization only
Disconnect
pauses the delegation: Gate One receives 403 delegation_disabled; the credential is kept
no
Erase
deletes the stored credential and metadata locally
no
Erase all my data
deletes every stored credential of the user
no
Erase is local only on purpose: the same credential may be used by the user elsewhere. To remove the application authorization itself, the user revokes it at the provider, in the provider’s own settings. The broker never calls the provider on erase (there is no revocation endpoint in the registry).
Rows are listed even when their provider is disabled or removed from providers.json: the user can still Erase them.
Where the code lives The reference implementation is services/token-broker/ in the Gate One source repository, and it ships as services_<version>_src.tar.gz in each release. It is a small Node.js service with its own Dockerfile; it is not part of the gate-one binary.
Install it The broker runs as a separate container, reachable only from the internal network:
docker build -t gate-one-token-broker services/token-broker docker run -d --name token-broker \ --network internal \ --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:size=16m,mode=1777 \ --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \ -e TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET=... \ -e TOKEN_BROKER_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \ -e TOKEN_BROKER_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://login.example.com \ -e TOKEN_BROKER_RETURN_TO_HOSTS=.example.com \ -e GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=... \ -v token_broker_data:/data \ gate-one-token-broker No published port and no ingress route: the broker is on the internal network only. Gate One reaches it at tokenBroker.url (default http://token-broker:4000).
Browser routes (/connections, /connect/, /oauth/) are published through the login host and served by Gate One: set tokenBroker.browserHost; Gate One authenticates the user with the configured provider and injects the identity. Do not expose the broker itself.
Only Gate One holds TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET (with the broker itself). auth-bridge no longer receives it: its legacy broker routes are inert (503). An ingress may route the login host to Gate One, but it must never proxy the browser routes directly to the broker: the broker would answer 401 without the secret.
State: the encrypted SQLite store lives on the /data volume; the key is in the environment, so a backup needs both the volume and the key.
Hardening: read-only root, dropped capabilities, non-root user.
Note Environment variables (all optional unless marked):
Variable Required Purpose TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET
yes
internal X-Broker-Secret shared with Gate One
TOKEN_BROKER_ENCRYPTION_KEY
yes
AES-256-GCM key, 32 bytes base64
TOKEN_BROKER_PUBLIC_BASE_URL
no
public login origin (callback/connect URLs)
TOKEN_BROKER_RETURN_TO_HOSTS
no
comma list of allowed returnTo hosts
TOKEN_BROKER_DB_PATH
no
SQLite path (default /data/token-broker.db)
TOKEN_BROKER_PROVIDERS_FILE
no
registry path (default /app/providers.json)
TOKEN_BROKER_STATE_TTL_SECONDS
no
authorization state lifetime (default 600)
TOKEN_BROKER_REFRESH_SKEW_SECONDS
no
refresh this long before expiry (default 60)
TOKEN_BROKER_HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
no
provider HTTP timeout (default 15)
TOKEN_BROKER_ADMIN_SECRET
no
operator API secret (X-Broker-Admin-Secret). Absent = admin API disabled (404). Gate One does not hold it
TOKEN_BROKER_RETENTION_DAYS
no
erase paused connections after N days. 0 (default) = keep forever; active delegations are never purged
Add a delegation service A provider is a registry entry, not code. Edit providers.json:
{ "providers": { "github": { "enabled": true, "display_name": "GitHub", "type": "oauth2", "authorization_endpoint": "https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize", "token_endpoint": "https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token", "client_id": "Iv23li...", "client_secret_env": "GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET", "scopes": [], "pkce": false, "refresh": true, "token_auth_method": "client_secret_post" } } } Field Meaning enabled
disabled providers are neither advertised nor require a secret
type
oauth2
authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint
HTTPS (HTTP only on loopback)
client_id
provider client id
client_secret_env
environment variable holding the secret (never inline)
scopes
requested scopes; [] for GitHub App permissions
pkce
send S256 PKCE (default true)
refresh
allow the refresh-token grant (default true)
token_auth_method
client_secret_post (default), client_secret_basic or none
authorization_params
extra string parameters; protocol params cannot be overridden
Adding Google, Slack or an internal OAuth service is a registry entry, not a code change. Only genuinely non-standard providers need an adapter.
Gate One references the provider name (routes[].upstream.tokenBroker.provider) and never sees its secret.
Endpoints Method Path Purpose GET
/health
liveness/readiness (no auth)

/connections/{provider}/disconnect
pause the delegation (no delete, no provider call)

/connections/{provider}/connect
resume a paused delegation (OAuth fallback)

GET

GET/POST/DELETE

operator API (separate admin secret)
/token/{provider} answers 200 with the access token, 404 not_connected, 403 delegation_disabled (the user paused the delegation; the credential is kept), 409 reauthorization_required (refresh rejected; the row is deleted) or 502 upstream_unavailable — each non-200 with a connect_url.
Link it to Gate One Gate One declares the broker once and a provider per route:
"tokenBroker": { "url": "http://token-broker:4000", "secretEnv": "TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET", "browserHost": "login.example.com", "links": { "services": { "label": "Services", "url": "https://login.example.com/connections" } } }, "routes": [{ "host": "api.example.com", "path": "/github/*", "backend": "https://api.github.com", "auth": {}, "upstream": { "tokenBroker": { "provider": "github" } } }] browserHost is the public host on which Gate One serves the browser routes. It may be omitted when links.services.url is an absolute URL: Gate One derives the host from it (here login.example.com). Set it explicitly when the link is absent, relative, or served by another host. If both are absent, Gate One does not serve the page; an ingress must never proxy those paths directly to the broker.
See Delegated credentials for the route details and the tokenBroker reference.
Operator API Set TOKEN_BROKER_ADMIN_SECRET and call the admin endpoints with X-Broker-Admin-Secret from the internal network:
curl -H "X-Broker-Admin-Secret: $ADMIN" http://token-broker:4000/admin/users curl -H "X-Broker-Admin-Secret: $ADMIN" \ http://token-broker:4000/admin/users/<sub> curl -X POST -H "X-Broker-Admin-Secret: $ADMIN" \ http://token-broker:4000/admin/users/<sub>/github/pause curl -X DELETE -H "X-Broker-Admin-Secret: $ADMIN" \ http://token-broker:4000/admin/users/<sub> The operator can list users and connections, pause/resume a delegation, and delete credentials, but cannot add or replace a credential: no write endpoint exists. Responses never contain a token value. Every admin action is audited in the broker log.
The operator API is disabled when the secret is absent. The broker must stay on the internal network: the admin secret is the only credential.
The shared secret is a bearer secret: it proves that the caller knows it, not who the caller is. That is why only Gate One (and the broker) may hold it; the infrastructure check refuses a configuration where another service (auth-bridge included) receives TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET. The browser routes are always served by Gate One, never by a second proxy pointing at the broker.
Security posture GET /security (shared secret) returns a redacted view for gate-one doctor and the infrastructure checks: public base URL, returnTo hosts, encryption enabled, admin API enabled, retention, database permissions, enabled providers (HTTPS, PKCE, refresh, auth method), token/user/paused/orphan counts. No secret and no token value is returned.
The broker never validates the quality of the shared secret or of the provider secrets: that belongs to the deployment/provider. It does enforce the functional gates: secret present, AES key = 32 bytes, HTTPS endpoints, strict provider fields, local file permissions.
Licence The broker is part of the Gate One distribution and follows the repository licence; it is not an authentication adapter. See Source and licence.

This example runs several Gate One replicas behind a load balancer and uses Redis as the shared OIDC session/revocation store. It is the multi-instance variant of the multi-app SSO example.
File examples/high-availability/routes.json
{ "authProvider": { "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/realms/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com", "sessionKeyEnv": "OIDC_SESSION_KEY", "sessionStore": { "type": "redis", "url": "redis://redis:6379/0", "passwordEnv": "REDIS_PASSWORD", "prefix": "cladone:auth:v1:" } }, "routes": [{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } Run it The packaged demo runs two Gate One instances, two tenants, two IAMs and Redis (Docker Compose):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/redis BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/redis](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/redis) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
export OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=... export OIDC_SESSION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" export REDIS_PASSWORD=... gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json OIDC_SESSION_KEY must be identical on every Gate One replica: it signs the shared session cookie. The Redis URL and password are also shared.
When to use it When you need horizontal scaling using several Gate One replicas behind a load balancer.
Single-instance alternative A single Gate One instance keeps the default bbolt store. See multi-app SSO for that simpler setup.
Failure mode When sessionStore is Redis and Redis is unavailable, authenticated routes fail with 502 authentication_unavailable. Public routes keep working.
Sentinel, TLS and ACL authentication are configured in authProvider.sessionStore.

Useful if you want to… give MCP clients (an assistant, an IDE, an agent) a governed tool surface over services that do not speak MCP;
expose a documented REST API as MCP tools without writing a server;
proxy an existing MCP server and restrict which tools it exposes;
aggregate several services under one endpoint with its own audience, scope and identity rules.
One endpoint, three sources An MCP route (mcp.enabled) builds its tool list one of three ways:
Source What you declare Derive from REST
mcp.operations names the tools; openapi.url resolves each operationId
Proxy an MCP server
mcp.upstream.url forwards to an existing Streamable-HTTP MCP server
Aggregate
mcpSets groups named services under one endpoint
The tools are derived from the route policy and the upstream OpenAPI document, not hard-coded per API: the same binary exposes any documented REST service as MCP.
Note The JSON below is a partial extract (one route or set), not a complete file. The runnable file is examples/mcp-tools/routes.json. Derive tools from an OpenAPI document { "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/github", "backend": "https://api.github.com", "auth": {}, "openapi": { "url": "http://landing/github-openapi.json", "public": false }, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "name": "github", "operations": [ { "name": "list_repos", "operationId": "list_repos" }, { "name": "get_repo", "operationId": "get_repo" } ] } } Gate One resolves each operationId in the OpenAPI document to the method, path template, parameters and JSON body schema, and turns them into the tool’s arguments. An unresolved operationId refuses the configuration at load, so a typo never ships as a silently missing tool.
Proxy an existing MCP server Instead of deriving local tools, forward to a server that already speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP:
{ "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/metrics", "backend": "http://metrics-mcp:8080", "auth": {}, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "name": "metrics", "upstream": { "url": "http://metrics-mcp:8080/mcp", "tools": { "include": ["list_*", "get_*"], "exclude": ["*_secret"] } } } } include and exclude are glob patterns over tool names; exclude always wins, and a hidden tool is refused on both tools/list and tools/call.
Aggregate services under one endpoint mcpSets groups named services (mcp.name) under a single endpoint. The set carries the access rights; each member keeps its own path and tool filter:
{ "mcpSets": { "developer-tools": { "host": "mcp.example.com", "endpoint": "/developer-tools", "resource": "https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools", "scope": "mcp-tools", "identity": { "roles": ["developer"] }, "members": [ { "service": "github", "path": "/github", "tools": ["list_repos", "get_repo"] }, { "service": "metrics", "path": "/metrics" } ] } } } a member endpoint is host + endpoint + path;
tools is an allow-list; omit it to expose every tool of the service;
enabled: false skips a member entirely (its service is not even compiled), which is how you stage a service without removing it;
set mcp.standalone: false on a service that must exist only through a set, never on its own endpoint.
Note mcp.operations and mcp.upstream are mutually exclusive on a route.
The audience check fails closed: if the issuer does not put the resource in aud, configure an audience mapper (or mcpAudience).
A tool name must be unique per route; an unresolved operationId refuses the configuration at load.
Authenticate the upstream The tool call reaches the backend with one of:
static headers — upstream.headers, one shared value;
delegated credentials — upstream.tokenBroker injects the caller’s per-user token from the token broker. It requires the top-level tokenBroker block (the same name, at the root of the file); a route that declares upstream.tokenBroker without it refuses to load.
The upstream never receives the Gate One bearer. Delegation is what lets a tool call GitHub or GitLab as the user; see Delegated credentials.
Metadata, scope and audience Each endpoint serves /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource with its resource (audience), scope and tool list, and Gate One checks the bearer aud and scope before any tool runs. The rules are shared with protected APIs: see Protect APIs and MCP tools.
Complete example MCP tools shows a REST-derived service, a proxied MCP server, an aggregating set and delegated credentials.

Useful if you want to… let a route or an MCP tool call an external API as the user, not as a shared service account;
keep the provider’s client secret out of Gate One;
let every user reach the upstream with their own rights;
give users a page where they connect, pause and erase those services.
The two credential shapes When a route calls an external API, the credential can be:
static — one shared value for every caller, set with upstream.headers (for example a service token);
delegated — the signed-in user’s own token, obtained after they authorize the service once.
Gate One implements the delegated shape with the token broker. upstream.tokenBroker on a route tells Gate One to fetch the caller’s token from the broker and inject it into the upstream request. It applies to plain proxied API routes and to the REST/MCP tools a route exposes — see MCP tools.
Important If the upstream needs the same credential for every caller, do not delegate. Set it once with upstream.headers, for example: "upstream": { "headers": { "Authorization": "Basic ${SERVICE_BASIC_AUTH}" } } Delegation is only for credentials that belong to the individual user. A shared service account, a static bearer token or a Cloudflare Access service token is simpler and has no connection page to manage.
What delegation is not Delegation is not an identity provider and not SSO:
the IAM/IdP still decides who the user is (auth, auth.identity);
the token broker only stores a token the user granted for one upstream service.
The names are easy to confuse, so see IAM, IdPs and provider types for the cladone-auth IAM (an OIDC issuer/IAM), the http-bridge provider type and the token broker side by side.
The token broker and the connections page The token broker is a small, internal-only service: a registry of OAuth providers plus an encrypted per-user token store. It is never exposed directly; only its browser routes are published through the login host, served by Gate One (tokenBroker.browserHost, provider-agnostic). auth-bridge no longer holds the broker secret and cannot proxy them: only Gate One (and the broker) has TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET.
Users authorize a service on the connections page ("Service connections"). Gate One links to it from the user badge as Services, and shows that link only when an exposed route declares delegation.
For the user The link is always present when the token broker is configured, even if no route currently delegates: it is also where the user erases stored credentials.
Open Services from the user badge (or follow the connect_url a delegated call returned).
Next to the service (for example GitHub), choose Connect and authorize it at the provider.
The broker stores the token; the next call to a delegated route uses it.
Disconnect pauses the delegation. It does not delete the credential and does not contact the provider; Connect resumes the same credential.
Erase deletes the stored credential locally (and its metadata). The provider is not contacted: the same credential can still be used elsewhere. Erase all my data does this for every service.
If the token can no longer be refreshed, the connection is marked reauthorization required and Gate One sends the user back to this page (409 reauthorization_required for an API call, a redirect for a browser route). A paused delegation answers 403 delegation_disabled with the Services URL.
Stored rows whose provider was disabled or removed from the registry are still listed, with Erase only: the user can always delete their own data.
Add a delegation service A provider is a registry entry, not code: the token broker’s providers.json lists each OAuth 2.0 service (endpoints, client id, scopes, …). Adding GitHub, Google, Slack or an internal OAuth service is a registry entry; its client secret comes from the broker’s environment, never from the file.
Gate One only references the provider name (upstream.tokenBroker.provider). See the token broker for the fields and an example.
Declare delegation on a route { "tokenBroker": { "url": "http://token-broker:4000", "secretEnv": "TOKEN_BROKER_SHARED_SECRET", "browserHost": "login.example.com", "links": { "services": { "label": "Services", "url": "https://login.example.com/connections" } } }, "routes": [ { "host": "api.example.com", "path": "/github/*", "stripPrefix": "/github", "backend": "https://api.github.com", "auth": {}, "upstream": { "host": true, "tokenBroker": { "provider": "github" } } } ] } auth is required: the broker needs an authenticated user id.
provider is a broker provider name (github), validated against the broker at startup.
the token is sent as Authorization: Bearer … by default; set header and prefix to change the header or the prefix.
browserHost is where Gate One serves the connections page and the OAuth callback (/connections, /connect/, /oauth//callback), authenticating the user with the configured provider and injecting the identity. Empty = derived from links.services.url. The browser routes must not be proxied directly to the broker, and auth-bridge does not receive the broker secret.
the shared secret is read from the environment named by secretEnv and is never written in the file.
the operator can list connections (metadata only), pause/resume a delegation and delete credentials through a separate admin API (TOKEN_BROKER_ADMIN_SECRET, never held by Gate One). The operator cannot add or replace a credential.
retention is unlimited by default (TOKEN_BROKER_RETENTION_DAYS=0); when enabled, it only purges paused connections.
Note The tokenBroker block and the route are shown together because a route that declares upstream.tokenBroker requires the top-level tokenBroker block; without it the configuration is refused at load. This is a partial extract (the providers and other routes are omitted) — the complete file is examples/mcp-tools/routes.json. When the user has not connected the service Gate One never sends a request without credentials:
an API/JSON call gets 401/409 with a connect_url the client can open;
a browser (frontend) route redirects to the connections page.
Important Gate One never stores the provider’s client secret; the broker does, and only the broker talks to the provider’s token endpoint.
Disconnect pauses; Erase deletes locally; neither calls the provider. Revoke the application authorization at the provider if that is the intent.
Destructive actions are CSRF-protected (signed form token + origin check).
The broker is internal-only and protected by a shared secret read from the environment.
Reserved header names (Host, Cookie, X-User-, X-Forwarded-, X-Gate-One-*) are refused for header.
A delegated route requires auth: there is no anonymous delegation.

This example separates the browser session from machine tokens and exposes one MCP service with its protected-resource metadata.
File examples/protect-api-mcp/routes.json
{ "authProviders": [ { "id": "company", "type": "oidc", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/t/company", "clientId": "gate-one", "clientSecretEnv": "MYCOMPANY_OIDC_SECRET", "loginBaseUrl": "https://login.example.com", "cookieDomain": "example.com", "sessionKeyEnv": "MYCOMPANY_SESSION_KEY" }, { "id": "company-api", "type": "jwt", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/t/company", "jwksUrl": "https://auth.example.com/t/company/jwks.json", "audience": "https://api.example.com" } ], "defaultAuthProvider": "company", "routes": [ { "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }, { "host": "api.example.com", "path": "/v1/*", "backend": "http://api:8080", "auth": { "provider": "company-api", "identity": { "scopes": ["read:things"] } } }, { "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/mcp", "backend": "http://mcp:8080", "auth": { "provider": "company-api" }, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "path": "/mcp", "name": "things", "resource": "https://mcp.example.com", "scope": "mcp-tools", "operations": [{ "name": "list_things", "operationId": "listThings" }] } } ] } Try the API route TOKEN="$(curl -s -X POST https://auth.example.com/t/company/token \ -d grant_type=client_credentials \ -d client_id=... -d client_secret=... | jq -r .access_token)" curl -i https://api.example.com/v1/things \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" A token without read:things gets a 403 from the gateway; the request never reaches the API. An anonymous call gets a 401.
Try the MCP route curl -s https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource | jq curl -s https://mcp.example.com/mcp \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' The metadata advertises the resource, the scope and the authorization server. The token audience must match resource.
Note A jwt provider never hosts a login page and never issues tokens.
auth.when is technical and evaluated before authentication; auth.identity is evaluated after it.
The JWT provider validates the token signature and aud; it does not validate the upstream IdP directly.
mcp.operations and mcp.upstream are mutually exclusive. Use upstream to proxy an existing MCP server instead of declaring REST operations.

Two kinds of example:
Runnable — a packaged demo under deploy/local/ in the source repository starts the whole stack on *.localhost (no domain, no external account). ./run.sh prints the URLs. Configuration pattern — a realistic routes.json for a setup that needs an external service (Keycloak, Google, GitHub). It is schema-validated; adapt it to your infrastructure. Example What it shows Runnable Getting started The embedded development identity provider, its default users and a user badge. Yes, no Docker Direct OIDC One OIDC issuer used directly, with roles and scopes read from that issuer and no federation or IAM. Yes, Docker Multi-app SSO A second application added to the same provider and cookie domain, reusing the login session. Yes, Docker Cross-domain SSO Unrelated domains sharing one IdP session, one provider per domain. Yes, Docker Embedded IAM cladone-auth federates an IdP, maps claims and stores user grants. Yes, Docker High Availability Several Gate One replicas behind a load balancer with shared Redis state. Yes, Docker Own account panel The application’s own burger panel reads the session instead of the built-in badge. Yes, no Docker Injectable UX User badge, UI gating, injection bundle and a nonce CSP. Yes, no Docker Usage plugin A signed audit plugin, a trust store, the WAL and per-type durability. Turnstile A public form and a whole-page gate protected by Cloudflare Turnstile, with the test keys. Needs internet Keycloak with Google A classical external IAM: Keycloak federates Google, Gate One trusts one Keycloak issuer. Pattern APIs and MCP A browser provider, a JWT provider, an identity-conditioned API route and an MCP service. Pattern MCP tools A REST-derived MCP service, a proxied MCP server and an aggregating set. Pattern IAM + IdP bridge An http-bridge provider returning identity and IAM facts. Pattern Enhance a proxied site An external site proxied through Gate One with an injected userscript. Needs internet The runnable demos live in the source repository under deploy/local/. They need the Gate One binaries (download a release and verify the checksums) and, for the OIDC demos, Docker Compose.

This example keeps Gate One’s frontend guard but removes the built-in user badge. The application provides a burger button and a side panel, then reads the session from Gate One.
Files index.html — application page and panel markup
panel.js — session, login and logout
panel.css — panel styling
routes.json — route without userBadge
README.md — run notes
Route { "authProvider": { "type": "dev", "loginBaseUrl": "http://login.demo.localhost:3000", "cookieDomain": "demo.localhost" }, "routes": [{ "host": "app.demo.localhost", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://127.0.0.1:8080", "auth": {} }] } There is no userBadge key. frontend: true keeps the guard, the login flow and window.__cladoneAuth available.
Read the session await window.__cladoneAuth.refresh({ quiet: true }); const session = await window.__cladoneAuth.session(); const name = session.claims.preferred_username || session.claims.email || "Account"; const roles = session.roles; const scopes = session.scopes; refresh() forces the probe because this route has neither a badge nor data-gtw-* markup. session() alone would wait for a probe that the guard never starts.
The direct probe is equivalent:
const res = await fetch("/__gate-one/auth", { cache: "no-store", credentials: "same-origin", }); const session = res.ok ? await res.json() : null; Run it The packaged demo serves the panel page and starts Gate One (no Docker):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/account-panel BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/account-panel](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/account-panel) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
# terminal 1: the application cd examples/account-panel python3 -m http.server 8080 # terminal 2: Gate One gate-one -check -config examples/account-panel/routes.json gate-one -config examples/account-panel/routes.json Open http://app.demo.localhost:3000/ and sign in with the development provider’s default users:
User Password alice
alice
bob
bob
Open the burger panel: it shows the username, email, roles and scopes. The top-edge Gate One badge is absent. Sign out calls window.__cladoneAuth.logout().
What to observe the route still redirects anonymous visitors to the login page;
the panel is rendered by the application, not by Gate One;
roles and scopes come from the same session the route policy uses;
after logout, the panel offers Sign in and the application stays usable.
Important The probe is display-only; server-side auth.identity remains the authorization boundary.
Account/services links and licence details are badge-specific and are not part of the probe. Define the links in your application.
A full-page reload after login is not required; login() resolves once the gateway session is active.

This example configures authProvider.type: "http-bridge" and points it at a service implementing the bridge contract. The bridge can adapt SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys or a legacy session service; Gate One only sees /auth, /auth/mcp and /health.
Important The bridge supplies identity and IAM facts (user, roles, scopes, claims), but Gate One remains the policy enforcement point. auth, auth.identity and MCP scope checks are still performed by Gate One on every request. The bridge never bypasses route policy.
The provider type remains http-bridge; http is its deprecated alias. The reference auth-bridge deployment is the IAM + IdP shape. A custom bridge may return only the authenticated user, in which case Gate One still enforces authentication but has no roles or scopes to check.
File examples/http-bridge/routes.json
{ "authProvider": { "type": "http-bridge", "baseUrl": "http://legacy-bridge:8080", "loginUrl": "https://login.example.com/login", "issuer": "https://auth.example.com/realms/example", "headers": { "userId": "X-User-Id", "username": "X-Username", "email": "X-Email", "roles": "X-Roles", "scopes": "X-Scopes", "claims": "X-Claims" } }, "routes": [{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} }] } Run it gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json The bridge must be reachable at baseUrl, expose the contract endpoints, and return 200 plus identity headers for an authenticated session.
Important The bridge owns the session; Gate One does not create an RP cookie for this provider.
A 5xx from the bridge is an outage (502), not a login failure.
Note Keep the bridge on the internal network.
The legacy type http is an alias of http-bridge.

This example builds one MCP surface from three sources: a documented REST API (derived into tools), an existing MCP server (proxied) and an aggregating set that groups both under one endpoint with its own audience, scope and identity.
File examples/mcp-tools/routes.json
Abridged (the authProviders and tokenBroker blocks are omitted here; they are in the file):
{ "mcpSets": { "developer-tools": { "host": "mcp.example.com", "endpoint": "/developer-tools", "resource": "https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools", "scope": "mcp-tools", "identity": { "roles": ["developer"] }, "members": [ { "service": "github", "path": "/github", "tools": ["list_repos", "get_repo"] }, { "service": "metrics", "path": "/metrics" } ] } }, "routes": [ { "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/github", "backend": "https://api.github.com", "auth": {}, "upstream": { "tokenBroker": { "provider": "github" } }, "openapi": { "url": "http://landing/github-openapi.json", "public": false }, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "name": "github", "standalone": false, "operations": [ { "name": "list_repos", "operationId": "list_repos" }, { "name": "get_repo", "operationId": "get_repo" }, { "name": "list_issues", "operationId": "list_issues" } ] } }, { "host": "mcp.example.com", "path": "/metrics", "backend": "http://metrics-mcp:8080", "auth": {}, "mcp": { "enabled": true, "name": "metrics", "standalone": false, "upstream": { "url": "http://metrics-mcp:8080/mcp", "tools": { "include": ["list_*", "get_*"], "exclude": ["*_secret"] } } } } ] } How it fits together github is a REST-derived service: mcp.operations names three tools, openapi resolves their method, path, parameters and body.
metrics is a proxied MCP server: mcp.upstream.url forwards to it, and tools keeps only list_*/get_* (never *_secret).
Both declare standalone: false, so they are reachable only through the set.
developer-tools aggregates them at https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools; the set enforces the developer role, the audience and the mcp-tools scope, and limits the github member to two tools.
The github tools call https://api.github.com with the caller’s delegated token from the token broker, never the Gate One bearer.
Try it # The set advertises its own protected-resource metadata. curl -s https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource | jq # List the aggregated tools, then call one. curl -s https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' curl -s https://mcp.example.com/developer-tools \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call", "params":{"name":"list_repos","arguments":{}}}' The github tools answer with a connect_url until the user connects GitHub on the connections page; the metrics tools need no per-user credential.
Note mcp.operations and mcp.upstream are mutually exclusive on a route.
tools.include/exclude (upstream) and a member’s tools (set) are both allow-lists; exclude always wins.
A member with enabled: false is skipped, and its service is not even compiled (no OpenAPI fetch).
Delegation needs auth; the token broker is internal-only.
See also MCP tools

Useful if you want to… remove the top-edge user badge from an application you control;
show the signed-in user, roles, scopes or claims inside your own burger menu or side panel;
keep Gate One’s login guard, SSO session, logout and route policy;
keep the account UI consistent with the rest of the application.
Gate One does not need to render the account UI. The built-in badge is only a client of the same session probe your application can read.
Route configuration Omit userBadge from the route. Keep frontend: true:
{ "host": "app.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://app:8080", "auth": {} } Do not set userBadge: {}: an empty object is still a badge policy. Omitting the key disables the badge while the guard, the login flow and the session API remain active.
Read the session The gateway exposes a same-origin probe:
GET /__gate-one/auth 200 {"roles": [...], "scopes": [...], "claims": {...}} 401 when anonymous In the application:
const res = await fetch("/__gate-one/auth", { cache: "no-store", credentials: "same-origin", }); const session = res.ok ? await res.json() : null; if (session) { const name = session.claims.preferred_username || session.claims.email || "Account"; renderAccount({ name, roles: session.roles, scopes: session.scopes }); } The public JavaScript API is also available on frontend: true routes:
await window.__cladoneAuth.refresh({ quiet: true }); const session = await window.__cladoneAuth.session(); // {roles, scopes, claims} or null refresh() is important: a route with no userBadge and no data-gtw-* markup does not probe automatically, so session() alone can wait indefinitely. refresh({quiet:true}) forces the probe without showing the reconnection banner.
Render the panel The application owns the markup. Typical content:
session.claims.preferred_username and session.claims.email;
session.roles and session.scopes as chips or lists;
the claim fields your application actually needs;
a Sign in button and a Sign out button.
Use textContent, not innerHTML, for claim values: they come from the identity provider.
The step-by-step version is Own account panel. The complete browser files are:
index.html
panel.js
panel.css
routes.json
Login and logout document.querySelector("#account-login").onclick = () => { window.__cladoneAuth.login(); // no-reload login tab }; document.querySelector("#account-logout").onclick = () => { window.__cladoneAuth.logout(); // OIDC end_session navigation }; Call login() from a user gesture, such as the burger menu’s sign-in button. It resolves true when the session is active and false when the user abandons the login.
What the badge shows, and what the probe provides Badge content Available from the probe username, email, selected claims
yes, session.claims
roles
yes, session.roles
scopes
yes, session.scopes
logout
yes, __cladoneAuth.logout()
account/services/app links
no — define them in the application
licence state and details
no — badge-specific
The badge’s links are merged by the gateway from connector configuration. If the application must show the same links, keep the list in the application or expose them through a dedicated API.
Warning The probe is for display only. It does not grant rights: keep auth.identity and backend checks as the security boundary. Note Do not cache the probe. The Gate One PWA already excludes /__gate-one/ from its cache.
Refresh when the panel opens and after login; the session can expire while the page stays loaded.
If the application has a CSP, its own panel script must satisfy that policy. Gate One’s guard supports csp.mode merge, hash and nonce.
Tip If you cannot modify the application, inject the panel as a bundle instead; see Injectable UX. Configuration reference routes[.userBadge]

Files routes.json

Route { "host": "app.demo.localhost", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://127.0.0.1:8080", "auth": {}, "inject": "bundle.json", "userBadge": { "position": "right", "claims": ["preferred_username", "email"], "roles": ["admin"], "logoutLabel": "Sign out" }, "uiGate": [ { "selector": ".danger-zone", "roles": ["admin"] }, { "selector": ".beta-feature", "hidden": "before" }, { "selector": "[data-feature=export]", "auth": "before" } ], "authGuard": { "forbidden": { "banner": true } }, "csp": { "mode": "nonce" }, "pwa": { "enabled": true, "networkOnly": { "excludePatterns": [ "^https://idp\\.example\\.com/.*/\\.well-known/openid-configuration", "^https://idp\\.example\\.com/.*/protocol/openid-connect" ] } } } Bundle { "injects": [ { "name": "announcement", "target": "body-end", "when": "/dashboard", "file": "banner.html" }, { "name": "brand-style", "target": "head", "style": ".demo-brand{letter-spacing:.02em}" } ], "patch": [{ "selector": "[data-feature=beta]", "attrs": { "data-gtw-auth-hidden": "before" } }] } injects[].when targets a path prefix; file is read at load, relative to the bundle. patch appends the data-gtw-* attributes client-side on every guard evaluation.
Try it The packaged demo serves the gated dashboard and starts Gate One (no Docker):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/injectable-ux BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/injectable-ux](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/injectable-ux) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
python3 -m http.server 8080 gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Log in as alice (user) then bob (admin). The .danger-zone is only visible to admin; the .beta-feature is hidden before login; the export control opens a login tab and replays the action after login.
CSP csp.mode: "nonce" emits Gate One’s own policy and stamps inline scripts. If the application already sends a CSP, prefer csp.mode: "merge"; if the application forbids inline scripts, use hash or merge and keep application scripts external.
PWA and identity endpoints pwa.enabled wraps the route in a service worker that caches same-origin pages and assets. Any URL that carries identity must therefore be excluded with pwa.networkOnly.excludePatterns (JS regexes tested against the full URL). Otherwise the worker can serve a cached auth probe — a stale identity after login or logout — or replay a callback that carries a one-time code.
Always exclude:
the identity provider’s discovery, authorize, token, JWKS and end-session endpoints;
any token endpoint used by API or machine clients (OAuth/JWT), and the http-bridge login URL when the route uses that provider;
the Gate One callback (/auth/callback) and, with the embedded IAM, /t/<tenant>/callback, which carry code/state.
"pwa": { "enabled": true, "networkOnly": { "excludePatterns": [ "^https://idp\\.example\\.com/.*/\\.well-known/openid-configuration", "^https://idp\\.example\\.com/.*/protocol/openid-connect", "^https://idp\\.example\\.com/.*/end_session_endpoint", "^http://login\\.demo\\.localhost:3000/auth/callback", "^http://login\\.demo\\.localhost:3000/t/[^/?#]+/callback" ] } } Replace idp.example.com with the issuer host. See the routes.pwa.networkOnly reference.
Note UI gating is a UX layer, not authorization. Keep server-side auth.identity rules for real rights.
The guard cannot intercept a request the browser never sent.
Injection and CSP are per route; do not enable own: true unless the configured policy is complete for the application.
A PWA service worker must never cache identity endpoints; see PWA and identity endpoints.
