body:
Useful if you want to… meter or audit usage without putting code on the request path;
keep operational metrics (auth failures, errors, request counts) in your own system;
integrate a commercial or closed-source extension without granting it access to tokens or identities;
survive a plugin outage without losing the events you declared durable.
Events are produced only for subscribed types. If no plugin subscribes to request, Gate One produces no request event at all. Free/self-hosted Gate One is operational-only: it ships no commercial metering.
Event types Type Produced when Default durability request
after a response, if subscribed
best effort
auth
login, logout, callback, back-channel logout, revocation
zero loss
error
401/403/502/5xx, provider unavailable
window
billing
a billable unit (units/unitType, optional attrs)
zero loss
audit
reload, plugin load/revoke
best effort
audit records control-plane events: action is reload, reload_failed or plugin_load, with detail carrying the plugin name or the reload error. It is best effort and never blocks the operation it records: if the type is unsubscribed, no plugin matches, or the WAL is full, the event is dropped and logged — a reload is never refused for lack of audit space. Admin 403`s surface as `error events.
request and error cannot use fsync: "always": the proxy emitter cannot fsync before a streaming response. Use window_ms for them.
Important Subscribing to auth makes sign-in depend on the event bus. On a login, auth is fail-closed: if the event cannot be written (WAL full, onMaxLag: block, plugin behind, disk error), Gate One returns 503 before creating the session — the user cannot log in. Do not subscribe to auth in production unless you explicitly accept that a full or unavailable WAL blocks login. For a demo, an audit trail, or any non-critical use, subscribe to request and error instead: they are window/best-effort and never block a request.
A route can opt out of the bus entirely with "usage": false (default true): it is served normally but produces no event — no WAL reservation and no admission 503 on that route. Use it for control or monitoring routes (a status page, an events viewer) that must not pollute, or depend on, the event bus.
Event shape An auth event:
{ "schemaVersion": 1, "type": "auth", "ts": "2026-11-02T12:00:00Z", "instanceId": "gw-1", "epoch": "2026-11-02T11:00:00Z", "tenant": "company", "subjectId": "v1....", "host": "app.company.example", "action": "login", "sessionId": "...", "status": 200, "authResult": "ok" } A request event additionally carries the route, host and method:
{ "schemaVersion": 1, "type": "request", "ts": "2026-11-02T12:00:01Z", "instanceId": "gw-1", "epoch": "2026-11-02T11:00:00Z", "tenant": "company", "subjectId": "v1....", "host": "app.company.example", "route": "/api/orders", "method": "GET", "status": 200, "durationMs": 12, "bytes": 1024, "authResult": "ok" } Rules:
no token, cookie, raw query string, email or username;
route is the normalized pattern, never the raw URL;
host is the request host, without port. Routes are keyed by (host, path): host + route identify the route, so the same path served on two hosts is not ambiguous;
the user is an opaque subjectId: a per-deployment HMAC of the (issuer, subject) pair, so it is stable and not reversible. The secret is shared by every instance and held only by the producer; a plugin never receives it. The exact construction is in the developer documentation.
The application may receive the same identifier as a backend header:
X-Gate-One-Subject: v1.<base64url> It is added after authentication, never accepted from a client, and is not an authentication token.
Billing capture (events) A billing event carries a metered amount: units + unitType (request, token, byte, mcp_call), plus optional bounded attrs.
Note This event is operational: it goes to subscribed plugins and has no tariff, no budget and no invoice. To price a request, hold a budget before the backend call and deliver a settlement, see Metering and billing.
The cheapest and most accurate source is the backend, which knows what it actually consumed. It returns internal response headers:
X-Gate-One-Units: 1240 X-Gate-One-Unit: token X-Gate-One-Billable: {"units":1240,"unitType":"token","attrs":{"model":"gpt-4"}} X-Gate-One-Billable is an optional JSON shortcut (≤ 512 bytes). The gateway copies the values into the event and strips the headers from the client response; a client-supplied copy is stripped from the request. Prefer this path: no request-body parsing, the smallest record, the most accurate count.
When the backend cannot report, opt in to gateway capture for specific endpoints:
"usage": { "capture": [{ "hosts": ["app.company.example"], "routes": ["/api/process_stream"], "methods": ["POST"], "types": ["billing"], "query": ["coupes", "lang"], "body": { "paths": ["$.coupes", "$.model"], "maxBytes": 2048 }, "maxAttrsBytes": 1024 }] } Captured values appear as attrs: q.<name> for a query parameter and b.<path> for a body field. Everything is bounded: at most 8 keys, keys ≤ 32 bytes, values ≤ 256 bytes, total ≤ maxAttrsBytes (default 1024, max 2048). When a value is dropped or cut the event sets attrsTruncated: true. Sensitive names (token, password, secret, authorization, cookie, credential, session, …) are always skipped, and a body is parsed only when it is no larger than body.maxBytes.
Capture applies only to the event types listed in types (default billing), so high-volume request events stay small. Keep the WAL lean: prefer the backend header, allow-list a few query names rather than whole bodies, and use a content-addressed spool (not the WAL) for large payloads.
WAL and backpressure one WAL per (node, event type);
one cursor per (type, subscriber);
a node budget (50 MiB by default) split into per-type shares; the sum of shares must not exceed the budget;
admission reserves space before authentication and before the backend call;
a full durable share answers the affected route with a targeted 503, Retry-After and a usage_unavailable body;
healthz, readyz, the auth probe and the usage endpoints are exempt;
fsync: "always" (zero loss) appends and fsyncs before the response; a failed fsync is a 503;
fsync: "window_ms" groups commits; a crash may lose the current window;
a subscriber beyond maxLagBytes either blocks (503 until it catches up) or drops (cursor advances to the lag limit, events become evictable, the plugin is marked degraded);
a new subscriber starts at the tail; there is no historical replay.
Note usage.dir is local to each replica: it is that node’s own WAL. With several replicas behind a load balancer, give every node its own directory (and its own nodeId) — two writers on one directory would corrupt it. Each node delivers its events independently; there is no cross-node aggregation.
On a login, auth is fail-closed: if the event cannot be written, Gate One returns 503 before creating the session. Logout and back-channel logout are best effort: the revocation must succeed even if auditing fails.
Signed plugins A plugin is an out-of-process HTTP/JSON service. It is never loaded into the Gate One process and never decides authentication.
{ "usage": { "dir": "./usage-wal", "nodeId": "gw-1", "subjectSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_SUBJECT_SECRET", "pluginSecretEnv": "GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET", "trustStore": "trust-store.json", "types": { "auth": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "always" }, "error": { "shareBytes": 10485760, "fsync": "window_ms", "windowMs": 250 } }, "plugins": [{ "name": "com.cladone.audit", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9100", "manifest": "audit.manifest.json", "artifact": "audit-echo.placeholder" }] } } The manifest is signed (Ed25519) and declares the artefact digest, the dependencies, the host API and the event subscription; Gate One verifies all of it at startup against usage.trustStore. A manifest is authoritative for the subscription (events.types, filters, maxLagBytes, onMaxLag) and the licence feature. Filters can narrow by hosts, routes, tenants, methods and statusClasses. routes matches the path only, not host+path, so add hosts when the same path exists on several hosts. The complete example is routes.json, audit.manifest.json, trust-store.json.
The plugin-side contract — the signed assertion, the /health and /events endpoints, the reference cmd/plugin-audit-echo, and how to sign, install and revoke — is in Plugins and Publish and trust a plugin.
Licensing Non-auth, non-IAM extensions may be closed-source or commercial; a commercial plugin may declare licenseFeature and the host refuses to load it without that feature. The full terms are under Source and licence.
Important There is no public compile-time plugin API. Go plugin (.so) is not supported.
A plugin cannot add a pre-auth hook, register its own route, mutate the identity or change auth, securityHeaders, license, rateLimit or quota.
Plugins are internal-network services: no Traefik exposure, signed assertion, separate UID, no secrets in the environment, egress allow-list.
Long-term retention is the plugin’s policy, not the core’s.

body:
Gate One can price a request before forwarding it, refuse it when the customer’s budget is exhausted, and deliver the priced measure to an invoice backend. The measure is computed by the core; the invoice backend never re-rates.
Note This is separate from the event bus. Usage events is an operational, subscribed stream of request/auth/error events; metering is a billable path with a tariff, a hold and a settlement. A deployment can use either, both, or neither.
Useful if you want to… charge per API call, LLM token, sold item, byte, GB·h, seat, second of session time or MCP call;
stop a request before the backend when the budget is gone, instead of discovering the overrun on the invoice;
keep a signed, replay-safe copy of every billable unit, locally, and deliver it without blocking the request path;
run the same pricing online, behind a firewall, or fully air-gapped.
The chain flowchart LR R["Request
host + path"] --> A["Admit
metric → tariff
→ amount"] A -->|"402 if the
budget is short"| X["Refused"] A --> H["Hold
(signed allowance)"] H --> B["Backend call"] B -->|"2xx/3xx/4xx"| S["Settle
capture the hold"] B -->|"5xx"| L["Release
nothing is billed"] S --> O[("Outbox
bounded, local")] L --> O O -->|"signed batch"| I["Ingest
verify + dedup"] I --> V["Invoice backend"] I -->|"signed receipt"| O O -.->|"air-gap"| E["Signed export
+ receipt"] The request path only does steps it can do locally: rate, reserve, forward, settle. Delivery happens in the background; a slow or unreachable invoice backend never delays a request, and a full buffer is a 503, never an unbilled request.
Metrics A metric is a billable quantity. It is declared once, under usage.metrics, and referenced by a route with "metric": "code".
"metrics": { "api.request": { "unit": "request", "scale": 0, "maxDimensions": 2, "dimensions": { "route": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 64 }, "tier": { "type": "enum", "values": ["free", "pro"] } } }, "llm.tokens": { "unit": "token", "scale": 0, "dimensions": { "model": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 32 } } } } Field Meaning unit
What is counted: request, token, byte, gb_hour, seat, second, mcp_call, or any label your tariff uses.
scale
Decimal places of the quantity: 0, 3 or 6. A quantity is an integer at that scale (1.250 GB·h is 1250 at scale 3), so no floating point ever enters the amount.
maxDimensions
Upper bound on the dimensions attached to a measure.
dimensions
Declared keys with a type and, for enum, allowed values. Only dimensions the gateway can know before the backend call are used (route is available; tenant comes from the identity).
measurement
event (default) or periodic.
heartbeatSeconds
For periodic metrics, the emission period (10–3600, default 60).
Note measurement: "periodic" declares a continuous quantity (session time, storage, a seat) and is validated and priced like any other metric. The gateway does not yet emit heartbeats itself: a periodic metric needs a producer that records deltas. Do not declare one expecting automatic session-time billing.
One measure per request A route with "metric": "api.request" produces one unit per request, with the dimensions the metric declares. The idempotency key is derived from the request ID (req:<requestId>), so a retried record is deduplicated by the receiver and by the invoice backend.
Tariffs A tariff is a versioned rate table for one metric. The map key must equal version; the tariff in effect at the measure’s instant is the one with the greatest effectiveFrom that is not in the future.
"tariffs": { "api.request.v1": { "metric": "api.request", "version": "api.request.v1", "currency": "EUR", "effectiveFrom": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "charges": [ { "model": "unit", "amountMicro": 10000 } ] } } Five charge models are available. Amounts are in micro-units of the currency (10000 = one cent in EUR), computed with big.Int and rounded once:
Model Formula Use for unit
quantity × amountMicro
a flat price per request or token.
tiered
each tier applies to the portion inside it
graduated volume discounts (the first 1 000 units at one price, the next at another).
volume
the tier containing the total applies to the whole
a volume price that switches at a threshold.
package
whole packages, with optional freeUnits
1 000 API calls per block, the first 500 free.
percentage_of
quantity × rateBasisPoints / 10 000
fixedAmountMicro
commission on a sale: quantity is the base amount in currency minor units, rateBasisPoints is 1 = 0.01 %.
A charge can be restricted with filter on dimension values; "*" matches any value. The first matching charge wins.
"charges": [ { "model": "unit", "amountMicro": 0, "filter": { "tier": ["free"] } }, { "model": "unit", "amountMicro": 20000, "filter": { "tier": ["pro"] } } ] Signed pricing plugins Some prices cannot be expressed by a table: a per-request quote, a negotiated rate, cost plus a live exchange rate. Such a metric sets "pricing": "plugin" and names a plugin; the plugin answers with a signed decision.
"pricingPlugins": { "llm-pricer": { "url": "http://pricer:9300", "publicKey": "<base64 Ed25519 public key>", "timeoutMs": 50, "failures": 3, "cooldownSeconds": 30 } }, "metrics": { "llm.tokens": { "unit": "token", "scale": 0, "pricing": "plugin", "pricingPlugin": "llm-pricer", "fallback": "llm.tokens.ceiling" } } The decision is signed over a line payload (amountMicro, currency, price version, engine version, inputs hash), so the gateway verifies what it did not compute. Any failure — timeout, bad signature, negative amount, open circuit — falls back to the declarative tariff named by fallback, and logs:
PRICING FALLBACK metric=llm.tokens plugin=llm-pricer: context deadline exceeded (declarative llm.tokens.ceiling) The fallback is mandatory and named explicitly, and it is priced by version, not by the clock: a plugin outage cannot silently change the price over time. cmd/plugin-pricer is a reference plugin.
Admission and the local budget Before the backend call, Gate One prices the request and reserves the amount from a signed allowance. If the reservation fails, the request is refused before reaching the application:
Status error Meaning 402
insufficient_allowance
the allowance cannot cover this amount.
402
allowance_expired
the signed allowance’s period is over.
402
no_allowance
no allowance covers this tenant/metric.
503
billing_buffer_full
the outbox is full (onFull: block).
503
billing_unavailable
any other admission failure.
A document navigation receives a short HTML 402 page; an API call receives JSON. A backend 5xx releases the hold (the customer does not pay for a failure); anything else settles it.
The allowance is minted by the managed side and verified locally with usage.allowancePublicKey:
gate-one allowance -key issuer.key -tenant company -metric '*' \ -amount-micro 5000000 -expires 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z \ -out allowance.json "usage": { "allowanceFile": "./allowance.json", "allowancePublicKey": "<base64 Ed25519 public key>" } The gateway refuses to start with metrics configured and no signed allowance: it would otherwise serve unbilled traffic.
Records and idempotency A settled measure is appended to the outbox as a JSON record:
{ "schemaVersion": 1, "tenant": "company", "metric": "api.request", "quantity": 1, "scale": 0, "dimensions": { "route": "/api/orders" }, "idempotencyKey": "req:9c1f...", "at": "2026-11-11T20:31:02Z", "amountMicro": 10000, "currency": "EUR", "priceVersion": "api.request.v1", "engineVersion": "declarative@v1", "inputsHash": "sha256:...", "settlement": "settled", "status": 200 } The natural unique key is (tenant, metric, idempotencyKey). There is no separate deduplication table on the producer: a replay is refused by the receiver, and a purge leaves a tombstone so a late replay cannot resurrect a deleted record. settlement is settled or released.
Delivery The outbox is local to the node and bounded, so a partition cannot grow the disk without limit:
"outbox": { "dir": "./usage-outbox", "maxAge": "6h", "maxBytes": 536870912, "maxRecords": 50000, "onFull": "block" } onFull: "block" answers 503 billing_buffer_full once a bound is reached; drop discards new records with a counter (only for metrics you accept losing). Defaults are maxAge: 6h, 512 MiB and 50 000 records. Size maxAge to at least two transfer intervals so one outage does not fill the buffer; watch the pending counters (gate-one billing pending) and alert well before the bound.
Delivery is a signed batch to a receiver, or a signed export when there is none:
"sink": { "url": "https://billing.cladone.example", "secretEnv": "SINK_SECRET", "signingKeyEnv": "SINK_SIGNING_KEY", "batchWaitMs": 200, "exportDir": "./usage-export", "receiptPublicKey": "<base64 Ed25519 public key>" } the batch carries each record’s payload as base64url and its sha256, so a hash is exact in any language with no JSON canonicalisation; the batch signature excludes the timestamp;
the receiver verifies the signature and every hash, deduplicates, and answers with a signed receipt carrying the next committed offset;
gate-one billing ack -receipt receipt.json commits that offset; the outbox deletes only acknowledged segments. An export is never committed without a receipt.
Aggregation to the invoice Invoice backends bill in cents. A metric priced below one cent cannot be sent one record at a time, so the managed path aggregates pending measures per (tenant, metric, currency, price version) and rounds once before creating the invoice line. The gateway’s amount is authoritative: the invoice backend never re-rates.
Reconciliation and audit The managed service reconciles every settled amount against the measures it received and the invoice it produced. You do not need its internals to audit your side: the gateway can replay and export what it priced, with no receiver, database or network.
gate-one meter verify -config api-routes.json # replay the tariffs gate-one meter export -config api-routes.json -out audit.json gate-one meter check -file audit.json -publicKey <b64> meter verify recomputes every retained record against the tariff version it names (independent of the clock). A record priced by a plugin cannot be recomputed and is reported as opaque (use -strict to fail). meter export writes a signed JSON snapshot; meter check verifies the signature, every record hash and the body digest. Hand the snapshot to an auditor with the public key: they need nothing else.
If you run your own receiver (billing-byo), the same contract applies on your side: deduplicate by (tenant, metric, idempotencyKey), answer with a signed receipt, and commit only what a receipt acknowledges.
Migration from the event-bus billing type Two mechanisms coexist, and they are not interchangeable:
the billing event (section Usage events) carries units/unitType to subscribed plugins. It is operational: no tariff, no hold, no invoice;
metering (this page) prices the request, holds a budget and delivers a settlement record.
Moving a route from the first to the second is a configuration change, not a code change:
declare the metric under usage.metrics (its unit replaces the old unitType), the tariff under usage.tariffs, and a signed allowance;
add "metric": "code" to the route;
keep usage.dir for the event bus; metering has its own bounded usage.outbox (six hours, not thirty days) and its own usage.sink.
The event bus stays useful for auditing and plugins; do not size the metering buffer from the WAL retention.
Try it locally deploy/local/metering-audit runs the user-side half on one machine: a gateway, a signed allowance and no receiver, then meter verify/export/check including a tamper attempt. It needs only the gate-one binary and Python 3.

This example puts Gate One in front of a real external site and injects a userscript into every HTML page. The browser installs no extension and the upstream site contains no Gate One code.
The example is the Wikipedia+ demo, moved from the deprecated gate-one repository. It proxies the language editions of Wikipedia and adds a dark/light toggle and a reading-time badge.
Files The full example lives in the source repository:
examples/siteproxy/
routes.json
injects/bundle.json
injects/wikipedia-plus.user.js
injects/wikipedia-plus.html
README.md
The .user.js file is the canonical, userscript-manager-installable artifact. The .html file is its generated <script> wrapper, used by the injection bundle.
Route { "host": "{lang}.wikipedia.demo.localhost", "path": "/*", "backend": "https://{lang}.wikipedia.org", "frontend": true, "upstream": { "host": true, "rewriteRedirects": true, "rewriteBody": { "enabled": true }, "responseHeaders": { "remove": [ "Content-Security-Policy", "Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only" ] } }, "inject": "injects/bundle.json", "wildcard": { "lang": ["en", "fr", "de", "ja", "zh", "ru", "es", "it", "pt"] } } The full file lists 29 language editions. The wildcard expands one route into one public host per language and compiles the cross-edition rewrite map.
upstream.host: true sends the origin its own Host header.
rewriteRedirects and rewriteBody keep the browser behind Gate One.
responseHeaders.remove removes the origin CSP so the injected script can run. Only do this for a trusted origin and trusted injected code.
inject points at the bundle; it is relative to routes.json.
wildcard.lang is the allow-list of language labels. A label outside this list has no route.
The bundle is deliberately small:
{ "injects": [{ "name": "wikipedia-plus", "target": "head", "order": 30, "file": "./wikipedia-plus.html" }] } The long userscript is not embedded in this page; it lives in the example directory.
target: "head" only says where the <script> tag goes in the document — it is not a DOM selector. The Wikipedia+ script replaces the theme, builds its floating panel and positions the arrow relative to that panel at runtime. Placing content at a specific element is the script’s job; see Placing content at a specific element.
Run it cd gate-one-src ./bin/gate-one -check -config examples/siteproxy/routes.json ./bin/gate-one -config examples/siteproxy/routes.json Point the public hosts at the gateway, then open:
http://en.wikipedia.demo.localhost:3000/wiki/Cat This example needs outbound internet access to *.wikipedia.org.
What to observe the page is served from the real Wikipedia origin, through Gate One;
the Wikipedia+ panel appears even though the browser has no extension;
interlanguage links move between the proxified editions;
the route is public: there is no auth policy.
Warning CSP removal is a real weakening. Only inject trusted code into a trusted origin; the userscript runs in the page context with the page’s full origin. Note The userscript must be free-licensed and vetted. The Wikipedia+ script is MIT licensed and carries the original copyright notice.
Keep the generated .html in sync with the .user.js; edit the userscript, then regenerate the wrapper.
A frontend: true route also carries the Gate One guard; custom bundle entries start at order 30 (the guard is 10, the PWA is 20).
See also Injectable UX

The public key is in trust-store.json; the private key was discarded. Do not trust this key in production: generate your own key pair and sign the canonical manifest plus the artefact digest.
Run it The packaged demo starts the app, the reference plugin and Gate One (needs Go for the plugin):
cd gate-one-src/deploy/local/usage-events BIN_DIR=~/gate-one-bin ./run.sh The script prints the URLs and stops with ./run.sh down. See [deploy/local/usage-events](https://github.com/clad-one/gate-one/tree/main/deploy/local/usage-events) for the stack and its README.
To run it by hand instead:
The plugin is a separate service: Gate One verifies its manifest but never launches it, so you start it first. The reference plugin lives at cmd/plugin-audit-echo in the source repository.
# terminal 1: the reference plugin export GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" go run ./cmd/plugin-audit-echo -addr :9100 -name com.cladone.audit # terminal 2: Gate One export GATE_ONE_SUBJECT_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" export GATE_ONE_PLUGIN_SECRET=... # same value as the plugin gate-one -check -config routes.json gate-one -config routes.json Open the app and log in: the plugin logs the auth event. Request an unknown protected path to produce an error event.
What to look at the startup verification (signature, digest, host API, name allow-list);
usage-wal/auth and usage-wal/error: one WAL per type;
fsync: "always" on auth: a full share returns 503 and no session is created (fail-closed);
X-Gate-One-Subject on the backend request: opaque, not an email;
SIGHUP reloads the config and the plugin registration.
Note The placeholder artefact is not a runnable binary: it only lets the configuration validate. Use a real signed artefact for a deployment.
The manifest is signed by the publisher; the operator only adds the public key to the trust store. The full walkthrough is in Publish and trust a plugin.
request and error cannot use fsync: "always"; use window_ms.
A plugin that stops acknowledging eventually triggers onMaxLag.
Long-term retention is the plugin’s policy; the core only keeps what must be consumed.

title: Turnstile protection

body:
Useful if you want to… stop bots from submitting a public form without changing the application;
protect an application that has no authentication and no form (a public tool, an API-driven frontend) — the page or only its expensive action;
add the same check to several pages and hosts from one place;
keep the widget working on a page Gate One already proxies.
The block is platform-wide: one configuration entry, every matching page gets the widget or the challenge, every matching request is checked with Cloudflare Siteverify before the backend.
Three modes Mode Protects Mechanism forms (default)
form submissions
widget injected into the matching forms; every matching POST is verified
gate
whole pages or actions (paths)
a challenge at the original URL, then a signed 30-minute clearance cookie; later requests pass without a new Siteverify call
both
gate + form submissions
the gate applies, and form POSTs are verified too
gate is the right choice for an application with no form: there is no POST to verify, and the page itself must be protected.
Protecting a whole page { "turnstile": { "mode": "gate", "siteKey": "0x4AAAAAAA...", "secretEnv": "TURNSTILE_SECRET", "hosts": ["gram.example.com"], "paths": ["/*"], "exemptPaths": ["/mcp", "/openapi.json"], "clearanceTtlSeconds": 1800, "challenge": { "appearance": "interaction-only" } }, "routes": [ { "host": "gram.example.com", "path": "/*", "frontend": true, "backend": "http://gram:8000" } ] } GET / without a clearance is answered by a challenge page at the same URL (no redirect). The backend is not called.
The widget solves the challenge and posts the token to /__gate-one/turnstile/verify. With a Non-Interactive widget, interaction-only keeps it hidden (silent verification); set challenge.appearance: "always" to show its loading spinner.
Gate One verifies it, sets gate_one_turnstile (HttpOnly, 30 min) and redirects to /.
The page is served; the backend was called once.
Protecting only the action To keep the pages public (and indexable) and protect only the expensive endpoint:
"turnstile": { "mode": "gate", "paths": ["/api/*"], "exemptPaths": ["/mcp"], "preclearance": true } The page loads normally; the injected script pre-clears in the background. An API call without clearance gets 403 {"error":"turnstile_required"} with X-Gate-One-Turnstile: required; the script opens the challenge, exchanges the token and replays the request. The backend sees one call: the rejected request never reached it.
Forms "turnstile": { "mode": "forms", "siteKey": "0x4AAAAAAA...", "secretEnv": "TURNSTILE_SECRET", "paths": ["/contact/*"], "forms": ["form#contact"], "action": "contact" } The widget is rendered in the matching POST forms and the POST is verified before the backend. data-gtw-turnstile="off" opts a form out. both adds this verification to a gate.
Failure modes Situation Status Body Missing/invalid token (forms)
403
readable page or JSON
Missing clearance, navigation (gate)
403
challenge page at the original URL
Missing clearance, fetch/API (gate)
403
turnstile_required + X-Gate-One-Turnstile
Missing clearance, form POST (gate)
403
readable page (data cannot be replayed)
Invalid token at the verify endpoint
403
the challenge page again
Siteverify unreachable
503
turnstile_unavailable, Retry-After: 5
A Siteverify outage is fail-closed, but existing clearance cookies keep working (their signature is checked locally).
CSP Turnstile needs https://challenges.cloudflare.com in script-src (and script-src-elem when declared) and in frame-src. When a route declares a csp block, Gate One appends those sources automatically in nonce, hash and merge modes. Without a csp block, the page’s own policy (if any) must allow them.
The limitation to document The check covers only traffic that passes through this Gate One instance:
a second ingress (nginx, Traefik, Kubernetes Ingress, another Gate One deployment with its own config) that reaches the application directly bypasses it;
internal callers and a published port bypass it.
The invariant is: the application is reachable only through the verification point. Restrict the application’s network access to the Gate One instance and deny everything else.
A gate on / also blocks search-engine crawlers: if the site must stay indexable, gate only /api/.
Limits Tokens are single-use and expire after 300 seconds. Gate One consumes them; the backend must not call Siteverify again.
The clearance cookie lasts clearanceTtlSeconds (30 min by default); rotating the signing key invalidates every clearance.
The client IP is sent to Cloudflare for validation; mention it in the privacy notice.
Cloudflare’s site key is bound to a domain list: every public hostname serving the widget must be declared there.
Try it The source repository ships a runnable demo on *.localhost with Cloudflare’s test keys:
cd deploy/local/turnstile ./run.sh gate # whole page gated ./run.sh api # only the action gated See the Turnstile example.
